The government can be removed by a vote of no confidence, and the executive can dissolve the lower house and call early elections. Walter Bagehot described the Cabinet as the 'hyphen' or 'buckle' joining the legislature and executive.
Important features include a nominal and real executive, collective responsibility and close relationship between executive and legislature.

Features: (1) a nominal head of state (monarch or president) and a real executive (prime minister and council of ministers); (2) close relationship between executive and legislature - ministers are members of parliament; (3) majority party rule - the leader of the majority party becomes prime minister; (4) collective responsibility of the cabinet to the lower house; (5) individual responsibility of ministers; (6) leadership of the prime minister; (7) secrecy of cabinet proceedings; (8) dissolution of the lower house on the advice of the prime minister; (9) a recognised opposition (the 'government in waiting', with a shadow cabinet in Britain); and (10) political homogeneity of the cabinet (members usually from the same party or coalition).

Merits: harmony between executive and legislature; responsible government, as the executive can be questioned and removed; flexibility to change governments in emergencies without waiting for elections; representation of diverse groups in the cabinet; and political education through debates. Demerits: instability in multi-party and coalition situations (as in Italy and India in the 1990s); cabinet dictatorship when a party has a large majority; violation of the separation of powers; lack of expertise among ministers; and party discipline that weakens parliament.
In a presidential system, the president normally serves as the real executive with a fixed tenure and institutional separation from the legislature.

The presidential system is based on the separation of powers. The USA is the classic example (since 1789); others include most Latin American countries (Brazil, Mexico, Argentina), Indonesia, the Philippines, South Korea and Nigeria. The president is the head of state and head of government, elected directly or through an electoral college for a fixed term, and cannot normally be removed by the legislature except through impeachment for serious offences.

The president appoints cabinet secretaries, who are not members of the legislature and are responsible to the president, not to the legislature. The legislature cannot be dissolved by the president. Each branch has its own sphere, and checks and balances prevent one branch from dominating the others.
Important features include separation of powers, fixed executive tenure and an independently elected or separately constituted executive.

Features: (1) single executive - the president combines the roles of head of state and head of government; (2) separation of powers - the executive, legislature and judiciary are separate; members of one cannot be members of another; (3) fixed tenure of the president (four years in the USA) and the legislature; (4) the president is not responsible to the legislature, and the cabinet is responsible to the president; (5) checks and balances - presidential veto, legislative approval of appointments and treaties, control of funds, impeachment and judicial review; (6) the president cannot dissolve the legislature; and (7) the president is elected by the people (directly or indirectly), giving independent legitimacy.

Merits: stability (fixed terms), strong and decisive leadership, protection of liberty through separation of powers, the president can appoint experts as secretaries, and less dependence on party politics. Demerits: deadlock and conflict between the executive and legislature ('gridlock'), especially in divided government; rigidity (an unpopular or incompetent president cannot easily be removed); concentration of power in one person, possibly leading to authoritarianism (as in some Latin American and African countries); and less accountability between elections. Comparing the two, Juan Linz argued that parliamentary systems are more stable for new democracies, while others point to successful presidential democracies.
Democracy is government based on the political authority and participation of the people.

Democracy is government in which supreme power is vested in the people and exercised by them directly or through elected representatives, under free elections. Key elements include popular sovereignty, political equality, majority rule with minority rights, rule of law, fundamental rights, free and fair elections, accountability, independent judiciary, free press and multi-party competition.

Democracy is also a social and economic order based on equality, and a way of life based on tolerance, cooperation and respect for the individual. Contemporary theories include liberal democracy, elitist democracy (Schumpeter), pluralist democracy (Dahl), participatory democracy, deliberative democracy and social democracy. The spread of democracy has occurred in 'waves' (Huntington): the first wave (1828-1926), second wave (after 1945) and third wave (from 1974, in southern Europe, Latin America, Asia and Eastern Europe).
Citizens themselves participate directly in public decisions.

Direct democracy originated in ancient Athens, where adult male citizens met in the Assembly to make laws, decide war and peace and elect officials, many chosen by lot. Modern forms include the Swiss Landsgemeinde (open-air assemblies in two cantons), New England town meetings in the USA, and in India, the gram sabha, which consists of all registered voters of a village panchayat area (Article 243A).

Devices of direct democracy in modern representative systems: referendum (voters approve or reject laws or constitutional amendments), initiative (voters propose laws), recall (voters remove elected officials before their term ends) and plebiscite (a vote on a major political question such as sovereignty or territory). Merits: direct expression of popular will, political education, legitimacy. Demerits: impractical for large states, complex issues reduced to simple choices, possibility of manipulation and majority tyranny.
Citizens elect representatives to exercise public authority on their behalf.

Representative democracy developed in Britain and the USA and is the form used by almost all modern democracies. The people elect representatives through periodic elections, and the representatives make laws and policies. Representatives are accountable to the voters, who can replace them at the next election. J. S. Mill considered it the 'ideally best form of government'.

Electoral systems: first-past-the-post (simple majority in single-member constituencies - India, UK, USA, Canada), proportional representation (party list systems - Netherlands, Israel; single transferable vote - Ireland; used in India for the Rajya Sabha and presidential elections) and mixed systems (Germany, Japan, New Zealand). Problems include the gap between representatives and citizens, the influence of money and lobbying, party control and low participation between elections; solutions include decentralisation, participatory mechanisms and transparency.
Democracy encourages participation, accountability, peaceful transfer of power and protection of political rights.

Merits of democracy: (1) based on the principle of equality and dignity of every individual; (2) government is accountable and responsive to the people; (3) protection of rights and liberties; (4) peaceful transfer of power through elections, avoiding violent revolution; (5) political education and participation of citizens; (6) better decision-making through discussion and consultation; (7) promotes patriotism and a sense of ownership among citizens; (8) accommodation of diversity and resolution of conflicts; (9) legitimacy and stability; and (10) Amartya Sen observed that no major famine has occurred in a functioning democracy with a free press, because governments must respond to public pressure.

Democracies also tend to have better human rights records, are less likely to go to war with each other (democratic peace theory) and allow correction of mistakes through free debate and elections. Churchill's famous remark sums up the case: democracy is the worst form of government except for all others that have been tried.
Democratic systems may suffer from slow decision-making, populism, misinformation, costly elections or unstable party competition.

Demerits or criticisms: (1) rule of the ignorant and incompetent - Plato and Aristotle feared rule by the uneducated masses; (2) 'rule of quantity, not quality' - votes are counted, not weighed; (3) slow decision-making; (4) expensive elections and the influence of money; (5) party politics, factionalism and corruption; (6) populism - politicians may make unrealistic promises and adopt short-term policies; (7) tyranny of the majority (Tocqueville, Mill) and neglect of minorities; (8) instability with frequent changes of government in coalition systems; (9) manipulation through propaganda, misinformation and social media; and (10) elitist critics (Pareto, Mosca, Michels) argue that real power remains with a small elite even in democracies.

Marxists criticise 'bourgeois democracy' as serving the capitalist class. Many of these problems can be reduced through education, electoral reforms, strong institutions, a free press and protection of rights.
Dictatorship concentrates political power in a ruler or restricted group with limited effective political competition.

Dictatorship is a form of government in which power is concentrated in a single person or a small group, who rule without effective constitutional limits, accountability to the people or genuine elections. The term comes from the Roman 'dictator', a temporary magistrate given absolute power in emergencies for six months. Modern dictatorships include Hitler's Germany, Mussolini's Italy, Stalin's USSR, Franco's Spain, Pinochet's Chile, Idi Amin's Uganda and current authoritarian regimes such as North Korea.

Features: concentration of power in one leader or party; absence or suppression of opposition parties; control of the press and media; restriction of fundamental rights and civil liberties; use of force, secret police and propaganda; one ideology imposed on society; no peaceful method of changing the government; and often a personality cult. Scholars distinguish authoritarian regimes (which control politics but allow some private freedom) from totalitarian regimes (which seek total control over all aspects of life, as described by Hannah Arendt and Carl Friedrich).
Dictatorships can take different forms, including personal, military or single-party rule.

Types: (1) personal dictatorship - power held by one individual (Saddam Hussein in Iraq, Muammar Gaddafi in Libya, Idi Amin in Uganda); (2) military dictatorship - rule by the armed forces after a coup (Pakistan under Ayub Khan, Zia-ul-Haq and Musharraf; Myanmar under the junta, including after 2021; Chile under Pinochet; many African and Latin American countries); (3) single-party dictatorship - rule by one party (the Communist Party in the USSR, China, Vietnam, Cuba and North Korea; the Nazi party in Germany); (4) fascist dictatorship - extreme nationalism and totalitarian control (Mussolini, Hitler); and (5) theocratic dictatorship - rule by religious leaders (Iran's system has elements of this; the Taliban in Afghanistan).

Other forms include monarchical absolutism (Saudi Arabia), 'competitive authoritarianism' or 'hybrid regimes' that hold elections but manipulate them (as described by Steven Levitsky and Lucan Way), and 'benevolent dictatorship', a ruler who claims to rule for the good of the people (sometimes said of Lee Kuan Yew's Singapore, though it held elections).
Supporters sometimes claim rapid decision-making and administrative unity, but such advantages come with serious risks to rights and accountability.

Arguments made in favour of dictatorship: (1) quick and decisive decision-making without lengthy debates; (2) strong and stable government; (3) efficient administration and implementation of policies; (4) effective handling of emergencies, wars and crises; (5) rapid economic development (examples cited include South Korea under Park Chung-hee and China's growth); (6) national unity and discipline; (7) less expensive than democracy (no elections); and (8) leaders may be more competent than elected politicians.

However, these claims are questionable. Many dictatorships have been inefficient, corrupt and economically disastrous (North Korea, Zimbabwe under Mugabe); decisions made without debate can lead to catastrophic mistakes (Mao's Great Leap Forward); stability is often temporary and ends in violent upheaval; and any benefits come at the cost of freedom, rights and dignity. Amartya Sen argues that democracy and development are mutually supportive.
Dictatorship restricts political freedom and accountability and creates strong possibilities for arbitrary or abusive power.

Demerits: (1) denial of fundamental rights and civil liberties - freedom of speech, press, assembly and religion are suppressed; (2) no accountability - rulers cannot be removed peacefully; (3) arbitrary use of power, torture, imprisonment and killing of opponents; (4) personality cult and propaganda; (5) corruption and nepotism; (6) suppression of minorities; (7) succession crises - no peaceful method for transferring power; (8) aggressive foreign policies and wars (Hitler, Mussolini); (9) lack of political education and participation of citizens; and (10) mistakes cannot be corrected because criticism is not allowed.

History shows that dictatorships often lead to great suffering - the Holocaust, Stalin's purges and famines, the Khmer Rouge genocide - and end in violent collapse or revolution. Lord Acton's dictum applies: 'Power tends to corrupt, and absolute power corrupts absolutely.' Hence most political theorists prefer constitutional democracy despite its imperfections.

Government is commonly analysed through three major organs. The legislature makes laws, debates public issues and controls finances. The executive implements laws and directs administration. The judiciary interprets laws and settles disputes.

The precise relationship among these organs differs between political systems. Parliamentary government creates close links between legislature and executive, while presidential government stresses institutional separation.

A functioning constitutional system requires these organs to perform their roles while preventing uncontrolled concentration of power.

Legislature: makes laws, controls finances, controls the executive, deliberates on public issues, amends the constitution and performs electoral and judicial functions; may be unicameral or bicameral; in parliamentary systems, the lower house controls the government through confidence; the 'decline of legislatures' due to executive dominance and party discipline is a concern. Executive: implements laws and runs administration; nominal and real, single and plural, parliamentary and presidential, political and permanent executive; it has grown in power in the modern welfare state.

Judiciary: interprets laws, settles disputes, protects rights, guards the constitution through judicial review and issues writs; its independence is secured by appointment methods, security of tenure, fixed salaries, difficult removal, separation from the executive and contempt powers. Separation of powers (Montesquieu) and checks and balances (the US model) aim to prevent the concentration of power; parliamentary systems fuse the executive and legislature but maintain an independent judiciary.

Relationship: in India, the executive is responsible to the legislature; the judiciary reviews laws and executive actions (basic structure doctrine); and the legislature can remove judges and amend the Constitution within limits. Effective constitutional government requires each organ to perform its role while respecting the limits of the others, with mutual accountability.

A unitary government places ultimate constitutional authority at the central level. Local or regional bodies may exercise powers, but these powers normally derive from the central constitutional structure.

A federal system constitutionally divides authority between central and regional governments. Federal arrangements commonly require a supreme constitution and mechanisms for resolving disputes over powers.

The basic difference therefore concerns whether regional powers are constitutionally coordinate or ultimately subordinate to the centre.

Unitary government: all power is concentrated in the central government, which delegates powers to local units; single citizenship, integrated administration and flexible constitution; examples - UK, France, Japan, China. Merits: uniformity, efficiency, strong government, low cost, national unity. Demerits: concentration of power, neglect of local needs, overburdened centre, unsuitable for diverse countries.

Federal government: constitutional division of powers between central and regional governments, written and rigid constitution, supremacy of the constitution, independent judiciary, bicameralism with representation of units; examples - USA, Switzerland, Canada, Australia, Germany, India. Merits: accommodation of diversity, decentralisation, protection of liberty, local participation, suitability for large countries. Demerits: weak centre, duplication, expense, conflicts and possible separatism.

Comparison and India: the main difference is whether regional powers are constitutionally guaranteed and coordinate (federal) or derived from and subordinate to the centre (unitary). India is a 'quasi-federal' system - a 'Union of States' with a federal division of powers but strong unitary features (residuary powers with the Union, emergency provisions, single citizenship, Governors, All-India Services, Parliament's power to reorganise states). In practice, many countries combine elements of both, and decentralisation within unitary states blurs the distinction.

In a parliamentary system, the executive emerges from the legislature and remains politically responsible to it. The head of state and head of government may be separate, and collective ministerial responsibility is important.

In a presidential system, the president is normally the real executive with a fixed tenure and is institutionally separate from the legislature. Separation of powers is more pronounced.

Both systems can be democratic, but they organise executive-legislative relations differently.

Parliamentary system: originated in Britain; nominal and real executives; fusion of executive and legislature; ministers are members of parliament; collective responsibility to the lower house; government removable by a vote of no confidence; prime minister's leadership; dissolution of the lower house; examples - UK, India, Japan, Canada, Australia. Merits: harmony, responsibility, flexibility, representation. Demerits: instability in coalitions, cabinet dictatorship, weak separation of powers.

Presidential system: originated in the USA; single executive (president as head of state and government); separation of powers; fixed tenure; president and secretaries not members of the legislature; no responsibility to the legislature; checks and balances (veto, Senate approval, impeachment, judicial review); examples - USA, Brazil, Mexico, Indonesia. Merits: stability, strong leadership, separation of powers protects liberty, expert administration. Demerits: deadlock, rigidity, possible authoritarianism, less accountability.

Comparison and suitability: the parliamentary system emphasises responsibility and flexibility, while the presidential system emphasises stability and separation of powers. The Constituent Assembly of India chose the parliamentary system because of familiarity with British institutions, the need for responsibility over stability, and the desire to avoid conflicts between the executive and legislature in a diverse country (Ambedkar explained that the parliamentary system offers daily and periodic assessment of responsibility). Some have proposed a presidential system for India to ensure stability, but most scholars support continuing the parliamentary model with reforms.

sections.title: Democracy: Meaning, Types, Merits and Demerits

blocks.text:
Democracy rests on popular political authority. It may be direct, where citizens decide issues themselves, or representative, where elected representatives govern.

Its merits include participation, accountability, political equality and peaceful transfer of government. Possible weaknesses include slow decisions, electoral manipulation, populism and instability under some conditions.

Despite its imperfections, democracy seeks to make public power answerable to citizens.

Meaning and types: democracy is government based on the authority and participation of the people. Direct democracy (Athens, Swiss Landsgemeinde, gram sabhas; referendum, initiative, recall, plebiscite) and representative democracy (elected legislatures and executives; parliamentary or presidential; various electoral systems) are the main types. Democracy also has social and economic dimensions and can be liberal, social or participatory.

Merits: equality and dignity, accountability and responsiveness, protection of rights, peaceful change of government, political education, legitimacy, accommodation of diversity, and better outcomes in welfare (Sen's observation on famines). Demerits: rule of the incompetent (Plato), slow decisions, costly elections, party politics and corruption, populism, majority tyranny, manipulation and elite domination. Conditions for success: education, economic equality, social harmony, free press, independent judiciary, strong opposition, civic consciousness and tolerance.

Conclusion: despite its weaknesses, democracy is preferred because it makes public power answerable to citizens and allows mistakes to be corrected peacefully. Indian democracy, with its regular elections and institutions, has survived despite challenges, but requires continuous efforts to deepen participation, reduce inequality and protect rights.

sections.title: Dictatorship: Meaning, Types, Merits and Demerits

blocks.text:
Dictatorship concentrates political power in one ruler or a restricted group and limits meaningful political competition. It may appear in personal, military or single-party forms.

Supporters may claim that concentrated authority permits rapid decisions. However, dictatorship weakens political freedom, public accountability and institutional restraints on power.

Its central danger is that power can become arbitrary because citizens have limited peaceful means to remove or control rulers.

Meaning: rule by one person or a small group without constitutional limits, accountability or genuine elections; features include concentration of power, suppression of opposition and media, denial of rights, use of force and propaganda, and personality cult. Types: personal, military, single-party, fascist, theocratic, absolute monarchy and hybrid regimes; authoritarian and totalitarian forms.

Claimed merits: quick decisions, strong and stable government, efficient administration, effective crisis management, economic development and national discipline. Demerits: denial of liberty and rights, no accountability, arbitrary and abusive power, corruption, suppression of minorities, succession crises, aggressive wars, lack of citizen participation and inability to correct mistakes. Historical examples - Hitler, Mussolini, Stalin, Pol Pot - show the catastrophic consequences of unchecked power.

Comparison with democracy: dictatorship may appear efficient in the short term, but democracy is more legitimate, stable in the long run, respectful of human dignity and capable of self-correction. The worldwide spread of democracy after 1974 and popular movements against dictatorships (the Arab Spring, 2011; protests in Myanmar after 2021) show the desire for freedom, though democratic backsliding remains a concern.
Classical liberalism emphasises individual liberty, private property, limited government and freedom of contract.

Classical liberalism developed in the seventeenth to nineteenth centuries as a reaction against absolute monarchy, feudal privilege, religious intolerance and mercantilism. Key thinkers: John Locke (natural rights, limited government, consent), Adam Smith ('The Wealth of Nations', 1776 - the 'invisible hand' of the market and laissez-faire), Jeremy Bentham and James Mill (utilitarianism), Herbert Spencer ('The Man versus the State', 1884) and early J. S. Mill. It was linked with the rise of the bourgeoisie, commerce and industrial capitalism.

It sees the state as a 'necessary evil' and a 'night-watchman' whose functions are limited to defence, law and order, protection of property and enforcement of contracts. Economic freedom - free markets, free trade and private enterprise - is seen as the basis of prosperity and political freedom. Classical liberalism's revival in the late twentieth century is called neo-liberalism (Hayek, 'The Road to Serfdom', 1944; Milton Friedman; Robert Nozick), which influenced the policies of Margaret Thatcher and Ronald Reagan and the 'Washington Consensus'.
Its core features include individualism, negative liberty, limited state intervention and confidence in markets and civil society.

Characteristics: (1) individualism - the individual is the centre of society and has rights prior to the state; (2) negative liberty - freedom as absence of restraint; (3) natural rights to life, liberty and property; (4) limited government and constitutionalism - government based on consent, separation of powers and rule of law; (5) laissez-faire economics - minimal state intervention in the economy, free market, free trade and competition; (6) private property as essential to freedom; (7) rationalism - faith in human reason and progress; (8) tolerance, especially religious tolerance; (9) equality before law and equality of opportunity (not of outcome); and (10) a contractual view of society.

Criticisms: socialists and Marxists argued that classical liberalism served the interests of capitalists and ignored the poverty and exploitation of workers; the freedom of the market was 'the freedom of the fox in the hen-house'. The Industrial Revolution's social problems led to the development of positive or welfare liberalism.
Positive liberalism accepts a more active role for the state in creating conditions that allow individuals to develop and exercise meaningful freedom.

Positive (modern, social or welfare) liberalism developed in late nineteenth-century Britain in response to the problems of industrial capitalism - poverty, unemployment, poor housing, child labour and ill-health. Thinkers include T. H. Green (Oxford idealist, 'Lectures on the Principles of Political Obligation', 1882), L. T. Hobhouse ('Liberalism', 1911), J. A. Hobson, John Maynard Keynes ('The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money', 1936), William Beveridge (the Beveridge Report, 1942, the basis of the British welfare state), Harold Laski, John Dewey and John Rawls.

Green argued that freedom is 'a positive power or capacity of doing or enjoying something worth doing or enjoying', and that the state should 'hinder hindrances' to the good life, such as ignorance, poverty and disease. Keynes argued for government spending to maintain employment and demand, especially during depressions. Positive liberalism justified the welfare state, social security, public education and health, labour laws and progressive taxation. Franklin Roosevelt's New Deal (1930s) and post-war European welfare states reflected it.
It stresses positive liberty, welfare, social opportunity and government action where necessary to reduce barriers to individual development.

Characteristics: (1) positive liberty - freedom as opportunity and capacity for self-development; (2) the state as a positive good and agent of social welfare, not a necessary evil; (3) welfare state - education, health care, housing, unemployment insurance, pensions and social security; (4) regulation of the economy - labour laws, minimum wages, consumer protection, regulation of monopolies; (5) a mixed economy and Keynesian demand management; (6) social justice and equality of opportunity, including progressive taxation and redistribution; (7) democracy and participation; and (8) retention of individual rights, constitutionalism and private property.

Critics from the right (Hayek, Friedman, Nozick) argue that the welfare state restricts freedom, creates dependency, reduces efficiency and leads to big government ('The Road to Serfdom'). Critics from the left say welfare liberalism does not go far enough to end capitalist inequality. The Indian Constitution's Directive Principles reflect welfare liberal ideas alongside socialist goals.
Liberal feminism seeks equal rights and opportunities for women through legal, political and institutional reform.

Liberal feminism is the oldest and most mainstream form of feminism. Key thinkers and texts: Mary Wollstonecraft ('A Vindication of the Rights of Woman', 1792), arguing that women are rational beings who should receive the same education as men; John Stuart Mill and Harriet Taylor Mill ('The Subjection of Women', 1869), arguing for legal equality and suffrage; Elizabeth Cady Stanton and the Seneca Falls Convention (1848); and Betty Friedan ('The Feminine Mystique', 1963), who founded the National Organization for Women (1966).

Liberal feminism is based on liberal principles of individualism, equal rights, rationality and equality of opportunity. It argues that women's subordination results from legal and customary restrictions that prevent them from entering public life, and that these can be removed through reforms within the existing liberal democratic system - without overthrowing capitalism or the family.
Major themes include equal citizenship, education, employment opportunity, legal equality and removal of discrimination.

Core themes: (1) equal rights - women and men are equal as rational individuals and should have equal legal and political rights (suffrage, property, divorce, custody); (2) equal opportunity in education and employment, equal pay for equal work, and anti-discrimination laws; (3) the public-private distinction - liberal feminists focus mainly on the public sphere (law, politics, work), though they also support reproductive rights; (4) reform, not revolution - working through legal and political processes, lobbying and courts; and (5) individual choice and autonomy.

Achievements include women's suffrage, equal pay laws, anti-discrimination laws (Title IX in the USA, 1972), access to higher education and professions, and reproductive rights. Criticisms: radical feminists argue that liberal feminism ignores deeper patriarchal structures in family and sexuality; socialist feminists say it ignores class and capitalism; black and postcolonial feminists say it reflects the concerns of white, middle-class Western women; and it may encourage women to adopt male norms of success. Liberal feminism remains influential in policy-making, including India's legal reforms.
Radical feminism views patriarchy as a deep system of male domination embedded in social and personal relations.

Radical feminism emerged in the late 1960s and 1970s from the second wave of the women's movement and the New Left in the USA. Key thinkers: Kate Millett ('Sexual Politics', 1970), who defined patriarchy as the most pervasive ideology of our culture; Shulamith Firestone ('The Dialectic of Sex', 1970), who argued that women's oppression is rooted in biology and reproduction and proposed technology (artificial reproduction) to free women; Andrea Dworkin and Catharine MacKinnon (on pornography and sexual violence); Mary Daly ('Gyn/Ecology', 1978); Adrienne Rich; and Germaine Greer ('The Female Eunuch', 1970).

Radical feminists argue that patriarchy - the system of male domination over women - is the oldest, most fundamental and universal form of oppression, existing before class and present in all societies and institutions, especially the family, sexuality and culture. 'Radical' means going to the root of the problem. The slogan 'the personal is political' (Carol Hanisch, 1969) means that personal relationships - housework, marriage, sex, childbirth - are sites of power and politics.
It focuses on patriarchy, gender power, control over women's bodies and transformation of social relations.

Core themes: (1) patriarchy as a system of male domination over women in all spheres; (2) 'the personal is political' - power relations in the family and private life; (3) sexuality and the body - male control of women's bodies through rape, domestic violence, pornography, prostitution, beauty standards and control of reproduction; (4) consciousness-raising - women sharing personal experiences in small groups to recognise common oppression; (5) sisterhood - solidarity among women; (6) separatism - some radical feminists favoured women-only organisations and spaces, and political lesbianism; (7) critique of the family as an institution of oppression; and (8) celebration of women's culture and values (cultural feminism).

Contributions: radical feminism brought issues such as rape, domestic violence, sexual harassment and reproductive freedom into public debate, leading to laws and services (rape crisis centres, shelters for battered women). Criticisms: it is accused of treating all men as oppressors and all women as a single group, ignoring differences of race, class and culture; of biological determinism; and of separatism. Later intersectional and postcolonial feminisms emphasised diversity among women.
Multiculturalism addresses the political recognition and accommodation of cultural diversity within a political community.

Multiculturalism is both a description of societies with many cultural, ethnic, religious and linguistic groups and a normative theory or policy that seeks recognition and accommodation of such diversity. Canada was the first country to adopt multiculturalism as official policy (1971, under Pierre Trudeau; Canadian Multiculturalism Act, 1988), followed by Australia. Key thinkers include Charles Taylor ('The Politics of Recognition', 1992), Will Kymlicka, Bhikhu Parekh ('Rethinking Multiculturalism', 2000), Iris Marion Young ('Justice and the Politics of Difference', 1990) and James Tully.

Multiculturalism challenges the assimilationist model (minorities must adopt the dominant culture - the 'melting pot') and the liberal idea of a 'difference-blind' state. It argues that equal citizenship may require recognising cultural differences and group-specific rights. Critics include conservative nationalists (who fear loss of national identity), liberals such as Brian Barry ('Culture and Equality', 2001), who argue that group rights undermine individual rights and equality, and feminists who note that cultural practices may oppress women (Susan Moller Okin, 'Is Multiculturalism Bad for Women?', 1999). Leaders such as Angela Merkel and David Cameron declared in 2010-2011 that multiculturalism had 'failed'. India, with its diverse religions, languages and tribes, is often described as a model of multicultural accommodation.
It stresses recognition, cultural diversity, minority protection and debates over group-differentiated rights.

Features: (1) recognition of cultural diversity as valuable and legitimate; (2) the politics of recognition (Taylor) - misrecognition or non-recognition of a group's identity can cause harm and inflict a sense of inferiority; (3) group-differentiated rights - special rights for minorities such as self-government, language rights, exemptions from certain laws (for example, Sikhs wearing turbans instead of helmets), and representation; (4) minority protection against assimilation and discrimination; (5) cultural identity as important for individual well-being; (6) intercultural dialogue and mutual respect; and (7) the state should not be culturally neutral in a way that favours the majority culture.

Policy examples: bilingual education, recognition of minority languages, special representation, religious accommodations, affirmative action, autonomy for indigenous peoples and national minorities (Quebec in Canada, Catalonia in Spain, Scotland in the UK). In India, minority educational rights (Article 30), linguistic states, personal laws, the Sixth Schedule and reservations reflect multicultural accommodation.
Will Kymlicka develops a liberal theory of minority rights and argues that certain group-differentiated protections can support individual freedom and equality.

Will Kymlicka, a Canadian political philosopher, wrote 'Liberalism, Community and Culture' (1989) and 'Multicultural Citizenship: A Liberal Theory of Minority Rights' (1995). He argues that individual freedom depends on access to a 'societal culture' - a culture that provides meaningful ways of life across public and private spheres, including language, institutions and traditions - which gives individuals the 'context of choice'. Therefore, liberals should protect minority cultures.

He distinguishes two types of minorities: (1) national minorities - previously self-governing, territorially concentrated groups incorporated into a larger state (such as the Québécois, indigenous peoples, Catalans), who are entitled to self-government rights; and (2) polyethnic or immigrant groups, who seek integration with accommodation, entitled to polyethnic rights (such as funding for cultural associations, exemptions from certain laws). A third category is special representation rights. Kymlicka distinguishes 'external protections' (which protect a group from the larger society and are acceptable) from 'internal restrictions' (which limit the freedom of group members and are not acceptable). Critics include Chandran Kukathas (who favours toleration without group rights), Bhikhu Parekh (who says Kymlicka's theory is too liberal and Western) and feminists concerned about women within groups.
Communitarianism stresses the importance of community, social membership and shared values in shaping individuals and political life.

Communitarianism developed in the 1980s as a critique of liberal individualism, especially Rawls's 'A Theory of Justice'. Key thinkers include Alasdair MacIntyre ('After Virtue', 1981), Michael Sandel ('Liberalism and the Limits of Justice', 1982), Charles Taylor ('Sources of the Self', 1989) and Michael Walzer ('Spheres of Justice', 1983). Amitai Etzioni later developed 'responsive communitarianism' as a political movement in the 1990s ('The Spirit of Community', 1993). Its roots go back to Aristotle and Hegel.

Communitarians argue that individuals are shaped by their communities, traditions, families and shared values; that the common good is as important as individual rights; and that liberal theories based on abstract individuals neglect the social foundations of identity and morality. They emphasise civic virtue, social responsibility, participation and community institutions.
It criticises excessive individualism and emphasises social responsibility, community and the moral importance of social relationships.

Characteristics: (1) the self is socially embedded or 'situated' - identity is formed through community relationships and traditions; (2) the priority of the common good over individual rights in some cases, or at least balancing rights with responsibilities; (3) importance of shared values, traditions and moral understandings; (4) civic virtue and active citizenship; (5) critique of the 'neutral state' - the state should promote certain conceptions of the good life; (6) importance of intermediate institutions - family, neighbourhood, religious groups, voluntary associations; (7) social responsibility - rights must be accompanied by duties; and (8) concern about the social costs of excessive individualism, such as loneliness, family breakdown, consumerism and declining civic participation (Robert Putnam's 'Bowling Alone', 2000).

Critics argue that communitarianism can become conservative, majoritarian or oppressive towards minorities and women, since communities may have unjust traditions; that it is vague about which community counts (family, nation, religion?); and that liberals like Rawls (in 'Political Liberalism', 1993) also recognise the importance of community. In India, ideas of community are strong in politics, as in caste and religious identity and Gandhi's vision of village communities.
Communitarians argue that individuals are socially embedded and cannot be understood as completely independent of communities and shared practices.

Sandel criticised Rawls's idea of an 'unencumbered self' - a person who exists prior to and independent of their ends and attachments, choosing values behind a veil of ignorance. Sandel argues that we are 'encumbered selves', constituted by our attachments to family, community, nation and history; we cannot be understood apart from them. Therefore, Rawls's priority of the right over the good is mistaken.

MacIntyre argued that modern liberal society has lost a shared understanding of virtue and the good life, leading to moral disagreement; he called for a return to Aristotelian virtue ethics rooted in communities and traditions ('narrative unity of life'). Taylor criticised 'atomism' - the view that individuals are self-sufficient - arguing that the capacity for autonomy itself develops only within a society that values it. Walzer argued that principles of justice differ for different goods (money, office, education, healthcare) according to shared social meanings, rejecting a universal theory of justice. These critiques encouraged liberals to take community, identity and civic virtue more seriously.

Classical liberalism places the individual at the centre of politics. It stresses private property, limited government and negative liberty, understood mainly as freedom from interference.

Positive liberalism developed partly in response to social and economic inequalities. It argues that meaningful liberty may require education, welfare and other conditions that enable individuals to develop their capacities.

Both traditions value liberty, but they differ over the role the state should play in securing it.

Classical liberalism: emerged with the rise of capitalism and the struggle against absolutism and feudalism; thinkers - Locke, Adam Smith, Bentham, Spencer; principles - individualism, natural rights, negative liberty, limited government ('night-watchman state'), laissez-faire, private property, rule of law, free trade and tolerance. It created constitutional government and market economies, but its neglect of social conditions led to poverty and inequality during industrialisation.

Positive liberalism: developed from the late nineteenth century; thinkers - T. H. Green, Hobhouse, Hobson, Keynes, Beveridge, Laski, Rawls; principles - positive liberty, a welfare state, regulation of the economy, social justice, equality of opportunity, public education and health care, and progressive taxation, while retaining individual rights and democracy. It shaped the welfare states of Western Europe, the New Deal and the Indian Directive Principles.

Comparison and later developments: both value individual liberty, but classical liberalism sees the state as a threat to freedom, while positive liberalism sees it as an instrument for creating freedom. From the 1970s, neo-liberalism (Hayek, Friedman, Nozick) revived classical ideas, leading to privatisation, deregulation and globalisation (India's 1991 reforms were influenced by this trend). Contemporary liberals debate the balance between markets and welfare, and Rawls's 'justice as fairness' remains the leading theory of modern liberalism.

Liberal feminism seeks equality for women through reforms in law, education, employment and political rights. It works largely within liberal institutions and demands equal citizenship and opportunity.

Radical feminism argues that gender inequality is rooted more deeply in patriarchy and social relations. It therefore examines power within family, culture, sexuality and other areas often treated as private.

The two approaches share opposition to gender domination but differ in their explanation of its causes and the depth of change required.

Liberal feminism: based on liberal principles of reason, individual rights and equal opportunity; thinkers - Wollstonecraft, J. S. Mill, Harriet Taylor, Betty Friedan; aims - equal legal and political rights (suffrage, property), equal education and employment, equal pay, anti-discrimination laws and reproductive rights; methods - legal and political reform within the existing system. Achievements include suffrage and many equality laws. Criticisms: focuses on the public sphere and the concerns of middle-class women; accepts liberal capitalist structures.

Radical feminism: patriarchy is the root of women's oppression, present in all institutions, especially the family and sexuality; 'the personal is political'; thinkers - Millett, Firestone, Dworkin, MacKinnon, Daly, Greer; issues - rape, domestic violence, pornography, reproduction, beauty standards, compulsory heterosexuality; methods - consciousness-raising, sisterhood, women-only organisations, cultural transformation; some advocate separatism. Achievements include making violence against women a public issue. Criticisms: essentialism, ignoring differences among women, treating men as a homogeneous oppressor group.

Comparison: both oppose gender inequality, but liberal feminism sees it as the result of discriminatory laws and customs that can be reformed, while radical feminism sees it as a deep structural system requiring fundamental transformation of social and personal relations. Other strands - socialist feminism, black feminism, postcolonial feminism and ecofeminism - add analysis of class, race, colonialism and environment. In India, feminist movements combine legal reform (liberal) with struggles against dowry, rape and patriarchal violence (radical influences).

Multiculturalism addresses cultural diversity and asks how political institutions should respond to minority identities and communities. It stresses recognition and challenges the assumption that one cultural pattern should dominate public life.

Will Kymlicka develops a liberal defence of certain minority rights. He argues that cultural membership can provide an important context for individual choice and that some group-differentiated rights can be compatible with liberal freedom.

His model attempts to reconcile cultural diversity with individual rights.

Multiculturalism: recognises and accommodates cultural diversity; rejects assimilation and 'difference-blind' liberalism; emphasises the politics of recognition (Charles Taylor), group-differentiated rights, minority protection, and intercultural dialogue (Bhikhu Parekh). Adopted as official policy in Canada (1971) and Australia; debated in Europe. In India, multicultural features include linguistic states, minority rights, personal laws, the Sixth Schedule, special provisions for states (Article 371) and the celebration of diverse festivals and languages.

Kymlicka's liberal multiculturalism: cultural membership provides the 'context of choice' necessary for individual autonomy, so liberal states should protect minority cultures. National minorities deserve self-government rights; immigrant groups deserve polyethnic rights; under-represented groups may deserve special representation. 'External protections' are acceptable, but 'internal restrictions' that limit the freedom of group members are not. Thus Kymlicka reconciles group rights with liberal individual freedom.

Criticisms and debates: liberal critics (Brian Barry) argue that group rights violate equality and may entrench conservative traditions; feminists (Okin) worry about women's rights within groups; communitarians and others (Parekh) argue Kymlicka's framework is too tied to liberal values; and nationalists fear threats to social cohesion. Supporters reply that multiculturalism promotes equal citizenship, inclusion and peace in diverse societies.

sections.title: Communitarianism and the Critique of Individualism

blocks.text:
Communitarianism criticises theories that imagine individuals as isolated from social relationships. It argues that communities, traditions and shared practices help shape identity and moral understanding.

Communitarians therefore stress social responsibility and the common good alongside individual rights. Their critique is directed particularly at excessive individualism that ignores the social foundations of human life.

Communitarianism does not necessarily reject liberty, but it asks political theory to take community seriously.

Communitarian critique: Sandel (the 'unencumbered self' versus the 'encumbered' or situated self), MacIntyre (loss of shared virtue and tradition), Taylor (critique of atomism and the social sources of identity), and Walzer (spheres of justice and shared meanings) criticised Rawlsian liberalism for abstract individualism, the priority of rights over the good, and the claim of neutrality. They argued that individuals are constituted by communities, that the common good and civic virtue are essential, and that justice depends on community values.

Communitarian values: social responsibility, duties as well as rights, civic participation, family and community institutions, shared moral traditions and a politics of the common good. Etzioni's responsive communitarianism tried to balance individual rights with social responsibilities and influenced policies such as community service and character education.

Liberal response and evaluation: Rawls's later work ('Political Liberalism', 1993) acknowledged that his theory was political, not metaphysical, and that citizens hold different 'comprehensive doctrines'. Liberals argue that communitarianism risks majoritarianism and oppression of dissenters, minorities and women. The debate has enriched political theory by drawing attention to identity, community and the social conditions of freedom. Communitarianism does not reject liberty but asks that political theory take community seriously.
A political party is an organised group that seeks to influence or control government, normally through elections.

Political parties are organised groups of people with similar political views who seek to gain power through elections, form governments and implement their policies. Edmund Burke defined a party as 'a body of men united for promoting by their joint endeavours the national interest upon some particular principle in which they are all agreed'. Joseph Schumpeter described a party as a group whose members act in concert in the competitive struggle for political power. Components of a party: leaders, active members and followers (supporters).

Functions: contesting elections and nominating candidates; forming governments or acting as opposition; formulating policies and programmes (manifestos); aggregating and articulating interests; recruiting and training political leaders; mobilising and educating public opinion; linking citizens with government; and providing stability to democratic systems. Without parties, representative democracy cannot function in large societies.
Parties may be national or regional and may also be classified by ideology, organisation or social base.

Classifications: (1) by geographical reach - national, state or regional parties; (2) by ideology - left (communist and socialist parties - CPI, CPI(M)), centre (the Indian National Congress) and right (conservative, nationalist parties - BJP); (3) by organisation - cadre parties (small, disciplined, ideologically committed, such as communist parties) and mass parties (large membership, broad appeal); Maurice Duverger made this distinction; (4) by social base - class-based, caste-based (BSP), religious (Shiromani Akali Dal, AIMIM), ethnic or regional identity parties (DMK, AIADMK, Shiv Sena, TMC, MNF); and (5) by role - ruling parties, opposition parties; catch-all parties (Otto Kirchheimer) that seek votes from all groups.

Party systems: one-party (China - Communist Party), dominant-party (Congress in India 1952-1967, the LDP in Japan, the ANC in South Africa), two-party (USA - Democrats and Republicans; UK historically - Conservative and Labour) and multi-party (India, France, Germany, Italy).
India's party system combines national and regional parties and has changed across different periods of democratic competition.

Features of the Indian party system: (1) multi-party system with a large number of registered parties (over 2,700 registered parties, of which six are national and around 60 are state parties as of 2024); (2) one-party dominance in the early decades (the 'Congress system', 1952-1967) and again a dominant party since 2014 (BJP); (3) rise of regional parties based on language, region, caste and ethnicity (DMK, TDP, TMC, BJD, SP, BSP, RJD, Shiv Sena, NC, MNF); (4) coalition governments at the Centre from 1989 to 2014 (and dependence on allies since 2024); (5) lack of internal democracy and dynastic politics; (6) personality-centred politics; (7) defections (aaya ram, gaya ram); (8) factionalism; and (9) the role of caste and religion in mobilisation.

Phases (Yogendra Yadav's classification): the Congress system (1952-1967); the Congress-opposition system (1967-1989), with the Janata Party's victory (1977); the third electoral system of coalitions (1989-2014), with the National Front, United Front, NDA and UPA; and BJP dominance since 2014, sometimes called the 'fourth party system'. The party system reflects broader changes in Indian democracy, such as the rise of OBCs, Dalits and regional identities.
Recognition of national parties is governed by Election Commission rules and prescribed electoral performance conditions.

The Election Symbols (Reservation and Allotment) Order, 1968, governs recognition. A party is recognised as a national party if it fulfils any one of the following: (1) it secures at least 6 percent of the valid votes polled in any four or more states in a general election to the Lok Sabha or state assemblies, and in addition wins at least four seats in the Lok Sabha; (2) it wins at least 2 percent of the total seats in the Lok Sabha (11 seats) from at least three different states; or (3) it is recognised as a state party in four or more states.

Recognition gives benefits: a reserved symbol throughout India, free broadcast time on public radio and television, consultation in setting election dates and electoral rolls, the right to have 40 'star campaigners' (whose travel expenses are not counted in candidates' expenses) and access to electoral rolls. The Election Commission reviews recognition after each general election. In April 2023, the TMC, NCP and CPI lost national party status, and AAP gained it.
State-party recognition is based on Election Commission criteria connected with electoral performance within a state.

A party is recognised as a state party in a state if it fulfils any one of the following: (1) it secures at least 6 percent of the valid votes in the state in the last general election to the Lok Sabha or the state assembly, and wins at least one Lok Sabha seat or two assembly seats; (2) it wins at least 3 percent of the total seats in the state assembly or three seats, whichever is more; (3) it wins at least one Lok Sabha seat for every 25 seats allotted to the state; or (4) it secures at least 8 percent of the total valid votes in the state in the last Lok Sabha or assembly election (introduced in 2011, even without winning seats).

A recognised state party gets a reserved symbol in that state and other benefits. In Mizoram, the Mizo National Front (MNF) and the Zoram People's Movement (ZPM) are recognised state parties, and other parties include the Congress and the BJP. State parties play a significant role in Indian federalism and coalition politics.
Single-party dominance describes a system in which one party repeatedly dominates electoral politics despite the existence of opposition parties.

Rajni Kothari ('The Congress System in India', 1964) described the 'Congress system' as a one-party dominant system: the Congress won large majorities at the Centre and in most states (1952, 1957 and 1962 elections), but it was a broad, inclusive coalition of diverse interests, groups and factions (a 'party of consensus'), while opposition parties acted as 'parties of pressure' that influenced the Congress from outside. W. H. Morris-Jones described it as a 'dominance-coexistence' system. The Congress dominance was based on its role in the freedom struggle, Nehru's leadership, its organisation and its ability to accommodate different groups.

This dominance was challenged in 1967, when non-Congress governments came to power in several states, and broken in 1977 by the Janata Party. Since 2014, the BJP's victories (with majorities in 2014 and 2019) have led some scholars (Suhas Palshikar, Yogendra Yadav) to describe a new 'BJP system' of one-party dominance, though the BJP fell short of a majority in 2024 and relies on NDA allies. Similar dominant-party systems include the LDP in Japan, the ANC in South Africa and the PRI in Mexico (1929-2000).
Coalition politics occurs when two or more parties cooperate to form or support a government.

Coalition governments in India: at the Centre - the Janata Party (1977-1979, a merger of parties), the National Front (V. P. Singh, 1989-1990, supported by the BJP and Left), Chandra Shekhar (1990-1991, supported by Congress), the United Front (H. D. Deve Gowda and I. K. Gujral, 1996-1998), the National Democratic Alliance (Atal Bihari Vajpayee, 1998-2004), the United Progressive Alliance (Manmohan Singh, 2004-2014) and the NDA under Narendra Modi (since 2014, with the BJP's own majority in 2014 and 2019, and dependence on allies such as the TDP and JD(U) since 2024). Coalitions have also been common in states, beginning with the Samyukta Vidhayak Dal governments of 1967.

Features: a Common Minimum Programme; coordination committees; 'coalition dharma'; bargaining over portfolios; and the influence of regional parties. Effects: increased federal balance and representation of regional and social groups; consensus-based policy-making; but also instability (the fall of the Vajpayee government by one vote in 1999), policy paralysis and pressure from allies. Scholars such as E. Sridharan argue that coalitions became the 'new normal' in India's diverse party system.
The Communist Party of India represents an important left-wing tradition in Indian party politics.

The Communist Party of India was formed in 1920 at Tashkent (USSR) by M. N. Roy and others; communist groups held a conference in Kanpur in 1925, regarded by the CPI as its founding date. During the freedom struggle, communists organised trade unions (AITUC) and peasant movements (All India Kisan Sabha), but were banned at times and opposed the Quit India movement in 1942. After independence, the CPI led the Telangana armed struggle (1946-1951) and then took part in parliamentary elections, becoming the main opposition party in the first Lok Sabha (1952). In 1957, it formed the first elected communist government in the world in Kerala under E. M. S. Namboodiripad (dismissed in 1959 under Article 356).

In 1964, the party split: the CPI(M) was formed by those who criticised the CPI's closeness to the Congress and the Soviet line. Later, the CPI(ML) (Naxalites, 1969) split from the CPI(M). The CPI supported Indira Gandhi's Emergency (1975-1977). Its ideology is Marxism-Leninism, with goals of socialism, land reforms, workers' rights and secularism. Its influence has declined; it lost national party status in 2023. The Left parties have been strong in Kerala, West Bengal (Left Front government 1977-2011) and Tripura (until 2018).
The Bharatiya Janata Party is a major national political party generally located on the right of India's party spectrum.

The BJP was founded on 6 April 1980 by leaders of the former Bharatiya Jana Sangh (founded in 1951 by Syama Prasad Mookerjee), which had merged into the Janata Party in 1977. Atal Bihari Vajpayee was its first president. Its ideological roots lie in the RSS and Hindutva (cultural nationalism), with principles of 'integral humanism' (Deendayal Upadhyaya, 1965), Gandhian socialism (in its early years), a strong nation, cultural nationalism, and opposition to 'minority appeasement'. Key issues have included the Ram Janmabhoomi movement (L. K. Advani's Rath Yatra, 1990), the abrogation of Article 370 (achieved in 2019), the Uniform Civil Code and the Citizenship Amendment Act (2019).

Electoral growth: from 2 Lok Sabha seats in 1984 to 85 in 1989, 120 in 1991, 161 in 1996 (Vajpayee's 13-day government), 182 in 1998 and 1999 (NDA government), 282 in 2014 and 303 in 2019 under Narendra Modi (the first single-party majority since 1984), and 240 in 2024, forming the government with NDA allies. It governs many states and claims to be the world's largest political party by membership. Its supporters credit it with strong leadership, development and national security; critics raise concerns about majoritarianism, minority rights and centralisation.
The ECI is the constitutional authority responsible for the superintendence, direction and control of specified elections.

The ECI (Article 324) is a permanent constitutional body, established on 25 January 1950, consisting of the Chief Election Commissioner and two Election Commissioners (since 1993). It superintends, directs and controls elections to Parliament, state legislatures, and the offices of President and Vice-President. Its functions include preparing electoral rolls, issuing voter IDs, recognising parties and allotting symbols, announcing election schedules, enforcing the Model Code of Conduct, monitoring expenditure, appointing observers, conducting polls using EVMs and VVPAT, and advising on disqualifications.

The ECI's independence and impartiality are essential for free and fair elections. T. N. Seshan's tenure (1990-1996) made it a powerful institution. Recent issues include the appointment process (the 2023 Act), allegations of bias in enforcing the Model Code, debates about EVMs and the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls (Bihar, 2025), which raised concerns about deletion of voters. Public trust in the ECI is vital for Indian democracy.
The Act provides major legal rules concerning elections, candidates, electoral offences, disputes and related matters.

The Representation of the People Act, 1950, deals with allocation of seats, delimitation of constituencies (with the Delimitation Act), qualifications of voters and preparation of electoral rolls. The Representation of the People Act, 1951, deals with the actual conduct of elections: qualifications and disqualifications of members (Sections 8-11, including disqualification on conviction for certain offences - the Supreme Court in Lily Thomas v. Union of India, 2013, ruled that convicted legislators are disqualified immediately); notification of elections; nominations, scrutiny and withdrawal; election agents; election expenses (limits set by rules, currently up to 95 lakh rupees for Lok Sabha candidates in larger states); conduct of polls and counting; registration of political parties (Section 29A); election disputes through election petitions filed in High Courts (Section 80); and corrupt practices (bribery, undue influence, appeal on grounds of religion, caste or community - Section 123) and electoral offences.

Amendments have introduced disclosure of contributions to parties (Section 29C), the use of EVMs, voting rights for overseas Indians (2010, in person), postal ballots for certain categories, the Model Code-related provisions and the ban on exit polls during specified periods. The Act is the main legal framework for India's electoral process.
The anti-defection provisions seek to discourage elected legislators from changing party allegiance in specified circumstances.

Frequent defections in the 1960s and 1970s ('Aaya Ram, Gaya Ram' - named after Haryana MLA Gaya Lal, who changed parties three times in a fortnight in 1967) destabilised governments. The 52nd Amendment Act (1985), under Rajiv Gandhi, added the Tenth Schedule to the Constitution. A member of a House is disqualified if he or she voluntarily gives up membership of the party, or votes or abstains contrary to the party's whip without permission (unless condoned within 15 days). An independent member is disqualified if he or she joins a party, and a nominated member if he or she joins a party after six months.

The original law exempted a 'split' if one-third of a legislature party left; the 91st Amendment (2003) removed this exemption, so only a merger supported by two-thirds of the legislature party is protected. The Speaker or Chairman decides on disqualification; in Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu (1992), the Supreme Court upheld the law but made the Speaker's decisions subject to judicial review. Criticisms: the law curbs the freedom of legislators to express dissent, gives too much power to party leaders, and the Speaker's decisions are often delayed or partisan (the Supreme Court in Keisham Meghachandra Singh, 2020, suggested an independent tribunal). Defections through mass resignations and mergers continue.
Electoral reforms are measures intended to improve fairness, transparency, participation and integrity in elections.

Reforms implemented: lowering the voting age to 18 (61st Amendment, 1988); EVMs (nationwide since 2004) and VVPAT; Electors' Photo Identity Cards (1993); the anti-defection law (1985, 2003); disclosure of criminal records, assets and educational qualifications of candidates (Supreme Court in Union of India v. Association for Democratic Reforms, 2002, and PUCL, 2003); NOTA (2013); limits on election expenditure; the Model Code of Conduct; ban on exit polls during voting; immediate disqualification of convicted legislators (Lily Thomas, 2013); and the requirement for parties to publish criminal records of candidates and reasons for selecting them (2020).

Committees on electoral reform include the Tarkunde Committee (1974), Dinesh Goswami Committee (1990), Indrajit Gupta Committee on state funding (1998), Law Commission reports (170th, 1999; 255th, 2015) and the Election Commission's proposals. Pending issues include state funding of elections, transparency in political donations (the electoral bond scheme, 2018, was struck down by the Supreme Court in February 2024 as violating the right to information), decriminalisation, inner-party democracy, regulation of social media and paid news, simultaneous elections ('One Nation, One Election' - the Kovind Committee report, 2024, and the Constitution (129th Amendment) Bill introduced in 2024), and remote voting for migrant workers.
Communalism in politics involves mobilisation or conflict organised around religious community identities in ways that may weaken common citizenship.

Bipan Chandra ('Communalism in Modern India', 1984) defined communalism as the belief that because a group of people follow a particular religion, they have common social, political and economic interests, which are different from and opposed to the interests of followers of other religions. He identified three stages: (1) communal nationalism - followers of a religion have common secular interests; (2) liberal communalism - interests of different religious communities are different; and (3) extreme communalism - interests of different religions are mutually incompatible and hostile, leading to hatred and violence.

Communalism should be distinguished from religiosity: being religious is not communal; communalism is the political use of religion. Forms include political mobilisation on religious lines, communal riots, hate speech, discrimination against minorities, and demands for separate states on religious grounds (as in the Partition of 1947). Major incidents in India: Partition violence (1947), the anti-Sikh riots (1984), the demolition of the Babri Masjid (1992) and subsequent riots, the Gujarat riots (2002), Muzaffarnagar (2013) and Delhi (2020).
Possible causes include historical conflict, political mobilisation, prejudice, insecurity and manipulation of religious identity.

Historical causes: British 'divide and rule' policies (separate electorates in 1909, communal representation and the Communal Award of 1932), communal interpretations of history (portraying the medieval period as Muslim tyranny and the ancient period as a Hindu golden age), and the trauma of Partition. Political causes: vote-bank politics, mobilisation of religious identity by parties and leaders for electoral gain, and the role of communal organisations.

Social and economic causes: economic backwardness, unemployment and competition for jobs and resources; lack of education; segregation of communities in housing; prejudices and stereotypes; and fears of minorities about their identity and security. Other factors: the role of media and social media in spreading rumours and hate speech; the failure of the administration and police to act impartially; external factors (cross-border terrorism, international events); and religious fundamentalism. Communalism is a modern phenomenon linked with politics rather than an inevitable result of religious differences.
Remedies include rule of law, civic education, inter-community trust, constitutional equality and responsible political leadership.

Remedies: (1) strict enforcement of the rule of law and punishment of those who incite or commit communal violence; impartial police and administration; quick justice for victims (the Communal Violence Bill was proposed in 2011 but not passed); (2) secular education and textbooks that promote tolerance, scientific temper and a balanced view of history; (3) responsible political leadership - banning appeals to religion in elections (Section 123(3) of the RPA, 1951; the Supreme Court in Abhiram Singh, 2017, held that appeals to religion, caste or community of the voter or candidate are corrupt practices); (4) economic development and reduction of inequality and unemployment; (5) inter-community dialogue, peace committees and civil society initiatives; (6) responsible media and regulation of hate speech and fake news; (7) protection of minority rights and equal citizenship; and (8) promotion of composite culture and shared festivals.

Institutions such as the National Integration Council (1961), the National Commission for Minorities (1992) and peace committees in districts help in prevention. In Mizoram and other Northeast states, civil society bodies such as churches and youth organisations play a role in maintaining social harmony, though ethnic tensions also need careful management.
Regionalism is political mobilisation based on regional identity, interests or demands.

Regionalism refers to a feeling of loyalty to a particular region based on language, culture, ethnicity, history, geography or economic interests, and the political mobilisation that results from it. It can be positive (a sense of regional identity, pride and demands for development and autonomy within the nation) or negative (when it becomes parochial, hostile to others or secessionist).

Causes in India: linguistic and cultural diversity; uneven economic development and regional disparities (for example, between developed states like Maharashtra and Gujarat and backward regions like parts of Bihar and the Northeast); historical factors (princely states, colonial administration); geographical isolation (the Northeast); neglect by the central government; 'sons of the soil' movements over jobs and migration (Shiv Sena in Maharashtra, Assam Movement); the role of regional parties and leaders; and ethnic identity. The Constitution accommodates regionalism through federalism, linguistic states, the Sixth Schedule, Article 371 provisions and the Finance Commission.
It may involve demands for autonomy, statehood, protection of regional interests or stronger regional political representation.

Forms: (1) demands for separate statehood within India - the formation of Andhra (1953) after Potti Sriramulu's fast-unto-death, linguistic reorganisation (1956), Maharashtra and Gujarat (1960), Punjab and Haryana (1966), Northeast states (1963-1987), Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh and Uttarakhand (2000), Telangana (2014), and continuing demands (Gorkhaland, Vidarbha, Bodoland); (2) demands for greater autonomy (the DMK in Tamil Nadu, the Anandpur Sahib Resolution in Punjab, 1973, and state autonomy demands in Jammu and Kashmir); (3) inter-state disputes over boundaries (Belgaum between Karnataka and Maharashtra, Assam with its neighbours including Mizoram) and river waters (Kaveri, Krishna, Mahadayi, Ravi-Beas); (4) 'sons of the soil' movements against migrants; (5) secessionist movements (Khalistan in Punjab in the 1980s, insurgencies in the Northeast, militancy in Kashmir); and (6) regional political parties representing regional interests.

Regionalism has strengthened Indian federalism and given voice to regional identities, but its extreme forms threaten national integration. Balanced regional development, decentralisation, cultural recognition and dialogue are seen as solutions.
The Constitution provides safeguards and forms of reservation for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in specified political, educational and public-employment contexts.

Constitutional provisions: Article 15(4) - special provisions for the advancement of socially and educationally backward classes, SCs and STs; Article 15(5) - reservation in educational institutions, including private unaided ones (93rd Amendment, 2005); Article 16(4) - reservation in public appointments; Article 16(4A) - reservation in promotions (77th Amendment, 1995); Article 16(4B) - carry forward of unfilled vacancies (81st Amendment, 2000); Article 46 - promotion of educational and economic interests of SCs and STs; Article 330 and 332 - reservation of seats in the Lok Sabha and state assemblies (84 SC and 47 ST seats in the Lok Sabha); Article 334 - the time limit for legislative reservations (extended every ten years, now until 2030 by the 104th Amendment); Article 335 - claims of SCs and STs in services consistent with efficiency; Article 338 and 338A - National Commissions for SCs and STs; Article 243D and 243T - reservations in panchayats and municipalities; and the Fifth and Sixth Schedules for tribal areas.

In central government jobs, the reservation is 15 percent for SCs and 7.5 percent for STs (in addition to 27 percent for OBCs and 10 percent for EWS). In Mizoram, most Assembly seats (39 of 40) are reserved for STs because of the predominantly tribal population. Debates include the 50 percent cap (Indra Sawhney, 1992), sub-classification within SCs (allowed by the Supreme Court in State of Punjab v. Davinder Singh, 2024), the creamy layer, and reservation in the private sector.

Political parties organise electoral competition and connect society with government. India's party system includes national and regional parties whose recognition is governed by Election Commission criteria.

The character of the party system has changed over time. India experienced long periods of single-party dominance as well as stronger multi-party competition and regionalisation.

The party system is therefore an important indicator of wider changes in Indian democracy.

Nature of the party system: India has a multi-party system with national parties (BJP, INC, CPI(M), BSP, AAP, NPP), recognised state parties and thousands of registered unrecognised parties. Recognition is governed by the Election Symbols Order, 1968, based on vote share and seats. Parties can be classified by ideology (left, centre, right), social base (caste, religion, region, class) and organisation (cadre and mass parties).

Evolution: (1) one-party dominance of the Congress (1952-1967), described by Rajni Kothari as the 'Congress system'; (2) the decline of Congress dominance and rise of opposition (1967-1989), including the Janata Party government (1977-1980); (3) fragmentation, regionalisation and coalition governments (1989-2014), with the rise of the BJP, regional parties and parties representing OBCs and Dalits after the Mandal Commission; and (4) the re-emergence of a dominant party (BJP) since 2014, though dependent on allies since 2024. Regional parties have remained powerful in many states, such as Tamil Nadu, West Bengal, Odisha, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana and Punjab.

Problems and reforms: lack of internal democracy, dynastic politics, personality cults, defections, criminalisation, opaque funding and the use of money and muscle power. Reforms suggested include regulation of internal party elections, transparency of funds, state funding, strengthening the anti-defection law and decriminalisation. The party system is an indicator of the deepening of democracy and the representation of new social groups.

sections.title: Single-Party Dominance, Coalition Politics and Left-Right Parties

blocks.text:
Single-party dominance occurs when one party remains electorally predominant while opposition parties continue to exist. Indian politics experienced such dominance for significant periods after independence.

Coalition politics becomes important when no single party can command sufficient legislative support and several parties cooperate. Left and right political tendencies also shape party competition; the syllabus specifically identifies the CPI and BJP.

These patterns show the changing structure of political competition in India.

Single-party dominance: the Congress system (Kothari) - a broad consensus party, accommodating diverse groups and factions, with opposition parties influencing it from outside; based on the legacy of the freedom movement, Nehru's leadership and organisational strength; broken in 1967 and 1977. The BJP's dominance since 2014 is based on strong leadership, Hindutva and nationalism, welfare schemes, organisational strength (RSS network) and a weak opposition, though it lost its majority in 2024.

Coalition politics (1989-2014): governments of the National Front, United Front, NDA and UPA; features - Common Minimum Programmes, coordination committees, bargaining and the influence of regional parties; effects - greater federalism and representation, but also instability and policy compromises. Coalitions are also common at the state level and in post-poll alliances.

Left and right parties: the CPI (founded 1925, Marxist-Leninist, led trade unions and peasant movements, formed the first elected communist government in Kerala, 1957, split in 1964 into CPI and CPI(M), declining today) represents the left; the BJP (founded 1980 from the Jana Sangh, rooted in Hindutva and integral humanism, rose from 2 seats in 1984 to dominance after 2014) represents the right. The Congress occupies the centre. The changing balance of left, centre and right reflects shifts in Indian society and politics, from Nehruvian socialism to economic liberalisation and cultural nationalism.

sections.title: Election Commission, RPA 1951, Anti-Defection and Electoral Reform

blocks.text:
