The Election Commission administers elections within its constitutional mandate. The Representation of the People Act, 1951 contains major legal provisions regulating electoral competition and related matters.

The anti-defection law seeks to limit certain forms of party switching by legislators. Electoral reforms attempt to improve transparency, integrity and democratic participation.

Together these institutions and laws provide an important framework for India's electoral process.

Election Commission: constitutional body under Article 324; three members; functions - electoral rolls, recognition of parties and symbols, conduct of elections, Model Code of Conduct, expenditure monitoring, EVMs and VVPAT; reforms under T. N. Seshan; challenges - money power, criminalisation, misinformation, questions of independence. Representation of the People Act, 1951: governs qualifications and disqualifications, nominations, election expenses, conduct of polls, registration of parties, corrupt practices (including appeals on grounds of religion, caste and community) and election disputes.

Anti-defection law (Tenth Schedule): introduced by the 52nd Amendment (1985) and strengthened by the 91st Amendment (2003); disqualifies members who voluntarily give up party membership or defy the whip; exemption for mergers of two-thirds; the Speaker decides, subject to judicial review (Kihoto Hollohan, 1992). Criticisms: restricts dissent, gives Speakers partisan discretion, delays decisions, and has not prevented defections through resignations and mergers.

Electoral reforms: implemented - voting age 18, EVMs and VVPAT, voter IDs, disclosure of criminal records and assets, NOTA, immediate disqualification on conviction, expenditure limits; proposed - state funding, transparency in donations (after the electoral bonds judgement, 2024), decriminalisation, inner-party democracy, regulation of social media, simultaneous elections and remote voting. Together, these institutions and laws form the framework for free and fair elections in India.

Communalism uses religious community identity in political mobilisation and may produce mistrust or conflict. Its causes can include prejudice, political manipulation and historical tensions. Constitutional equality, rule of law and responsible leadership are important remedies.

Regionalism is mobilisation around regional identity or interests. It can take democratic forms such as demands for autonomy or stronger representation, but severe forms may create political tensions.

Both issues demonstrate the importance of managing social diversity within a democratic constitutional order.

Communalism: the belief that religious communities have separate and opposed interests; stages (Bipan Chandra) - communal nationalism, liberal communalism and extreme communalism; causes - colonial divide and rule, communal history, Partition, vote-bank politics, economic competition, prejudice, media and fundamentalism; manifestations - riots, hate speech, discrimination, polarisation. Remedies - rule of law and impartial administration, secular education, responsible leadership and legal bans on religious appeals in elections, economic development, inter-community dialogue, responsible media and protection of minority rights. Secularism (S. R. Bommai, 1994) is part of the basic structure of the Constitution.

Regionalism: loyalty to a region based on language, culture, ethnicity or economic interest; causes - diversity, uneven development, neglect, historical and geographical factors, regional parties and migration; forms - statehood demands, autonomy demands, inter-state disputes, sons-of-the-soil movements and secessionism. The States Reorganisation Commission (1953-1955), linguistic states (1956), new states (1960-2014) and special provisions (Articles 371A-J, Sixth Schedule) show how the Constitution accommodates regional aspirations.

Conclusion: both communalism and regionalism arise from India's diversity. Democratic and federal institutions can accommodate diversity, but when identity politics becomes exclusive and hostile, it threatens national unity and democracy. Managing diversity requires constitutional values, inclusive development, decentralisation, tolerance and responsible political leadership.

sections.title: Constitutional Reservation for SCs and STs

blocks.text:
The Constitution recognises the historical disadvantage faced by Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes and provides special safeguards and reservation in specified fields.

These provisions seek representation and substantive equality rather than merely identical treatment. Political reservation and other constitutional measures are part of the broader framework of social justice.

Reservation therefore connects democratic representation with the constitutional objective of addressing entrenched inequality.

Rationale: SCs (formerly 'untouchables', about 16.6 percent of the population in 2011) and STs (tribal communities, about 8.6 percent) suffered historical injustice - untouchability, exclusion from education and property, and geographical isolation. Formal equality would perpetuate their disadvantage, so the Constitution provides 'protective discrimination' to achieve substantive equality and representation, as part of social justice (Preamble, Articles 38, 46). Ambedkar and the Constituent Assembly considered reservations essential.

Provisions: reservation in legislatures (Articles 330, 332, extended until 2030), in local bodies (Articles 243D, 243T), in public employment (Articles 16(4), 16(4A), 16(4B), 335) and in educational institutions (Articles 15(4), 15(5)); the National Commissions for SCs (Article 338) and STs (Article 338A, created by the 89th Amendment, 2003); the abolition of untouchability (Article 17); the Fifth Schedule (Scheduled Areas) and Sixth Schedule (tribal areas of the Northeast); and laws such as the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act (1989), the PESA Act (1996) and the Forest Rights Act (2006).

Debates and evaluation: reservations have increased representation of SCs and STs in legislatures, government services and education, and created a new middle class among them. Criticisms include the benefits going mainly to the better-off sections (creamy layer debate - the Supreme Court in 2024 suggested a creamy layer for SCs and STs too), inadequate implementation (unfilled posts), reservations in promotions, the 50 percent ceiling, and the argument for economic criteria. Supporters argue that caste discrimination persists and reservations remain necessary. Reservation connects democratic representation with the constitutional goal of addressing entrenched inequality.
Public administration concerns the organisation and implementation of government policies and public programmes.

Woodrow Wilson's essay 'The Study of Administration' (1887) is considered the starting point of the discipline; he is called the father of Public Administration. He proposed the politics-administration dichotomy - politics sets goals, and administration implements them efficiently. Definitions: Wilson - 'detailed and systematic execution of public law'; L. D. White - 'all those operations having for their purpose the fulfilment or enforcement of public policy'; Luther Gulick - 'that part of the science of administration which has to do with government'; Dwight Waldo - 'the art and science of management as applied to the affairs of state'.

Public administration differs from private (business) administration in its aims (public interest versus profit), accountability (to legislatures, courts and citizens), legal framework, scale, monopoly of services and political environment, though both share techniques of management. Paul Appleby emphasised that public administration is different because of its political character and public accountability.
Its scope includes public organisations, personnel, budgeting, administrative behaviour, accountability and implementation of public policy.

Narrow and broad views: the narrow (managerial) view considers only executive activities (Gulick, Simon), while the broad (integral) view includes all activities of government - legislative, executive and judicial (L. D. White, Marshall Dimock). Luther Gulick's POSDCORB describes the managerial functions of the chief executive: Planning, Organising, Staffing, Directing, Coordinating, Reporting and Budgeting. Critics say POSDCORB ignores the substantive content of administration (the subject matter of departments like health, education and defence).

Modern scope includes organisation theory, personnel administration, financial administration, public policy, comparative and development administration, local government, administrative law and accountability, e-governance, public-private partnerships and governance. Approaches have evolved from classical theory to New Public Administration (Minnowbrook Conference, 1968, emphasising relevance, values, equity and change), New Public Management (1980s-1990s, emphasising market principles, efficiency, results and 'reinventing government' - Osborne and Gaebler, 1992), New Public Service (Denhardt) and good governance.
Administration connects government decisions with practical delivery of public services and is therefore essential to modern governance.

Significance: public administration is the 'heart of the modern state' (Brooks Adams said it is 'the capacity of coordinating many, and often conflicting, social energies in a single organism'). It implements laws and policies, delivers essential services (education, health, water, transport), maintains law and order, collects revenue, manages emergencies (disasters, pandemics), promotes economic development and social welfare, protects the environment, and provides continuity and stability even when governments change.

In developing countries like India, administration plays a key role in nation-building and development (rural development, poverty alleviation, welfare schemes such as MGNREGA and the Public Distribution System). The quality of administration determines whether policies succeed. Challenges include corruption, red tape, inefficiency, lack of accountability and politicisation; reforms aim at good governance, transparency (RTI), citizen charters, e-governance (Digital India, direct benefit transfers) and decentralisation.
Scientific management seeks efficiency through systematic study of work, specialisation and improved methods of organisation.

Frederick Winslow Taylor (1856-1915), an American engineer, is the father of scientific management ('The Principles of Scientific Management', 1911). Based on time-and-motion studies at Midvale Steel and Bethlehem Steel, he argued that there is 'one best way' to do any job, which can be discovered scientifically. Principles: (1) scientific study of each element of work to replace rule-of-thumb methods; (2) scientific selection, training and development of workers; (3) cooperation between management and workers to ensure work is done according to scientific principles; and (4) division of responsibility between management (planning) and workers (execution). He also proposed functional foremanship (eight specialised foremen instead of one) and differential piece-rate wages to motivate workers.

Others in the classical tradition include Henri Fayol (14 principles of management, such as division of work, unity of command, scalar chain and esprit de corps), Luther Gulick and Lyndall Urwick (POSDCORB), Frank and Lillian Gilbreth (motion studies) and Henry Gantt (Gantt charts). Criticisms: treats workers as machines ('economic man') motivated only by money; ignores human and social factors; leads to monotony and exploitation; and was opposed by trade unions. Nevertheless, it improved productivity and laid the foundations of management science.
The human relations approach stresses informal groups, motivation and social relationships within organisations.

The human relations approach arose from the Hawthorne experiments (1924-1932) at the Western Electric Company's Hawthorne Works near Chicago, led by Elton Mayo, F. J. Roethlisberger and W. J. Dickson of Harvard. The experiments included illumination studies (productivity increased whether lighting was increased or decreased), relay assembly test room studies (productivity increased due to attention and group cohesion - the 'Hawthorne effect'), interviews, and the bank wiring room study (informal groups set their own production norms).

Findings: workers are social beings with emotional needs, not just economic beings; informal groups, social relationships, morale, communication, participation and supervision style strongly influence productivity; non-economic rewards (recognition, belonging) matter; and the organisation is a social system. Later behavioural theorists - Abraham Maslow (hierarchy of needs), Douglas McGregor (Theory X and Theory Y), Frederick Herzberg (two-factor theory), Chris Argyris and Rensis Likert - developed these insights. Criticisms: overemphasis on human relations and informal groups, neglect of formal structure and economic factors, and potential manipulation of workers by management.
The bureaucratic approach analyses formal hierarchy, rules, offices, specialisation and impersonal administration.

Max Weber (1864-1920), a German sociologist, developed the 'ideal type' of bureaucracy based on legal-rational authority ('Economy and Society', published 1922). Characteristics: (1) hierarchy of offices with a clear chain of command; (2) a division of labour and specialisation; (3) a system of rules and regulations governing official decisions; (4) impersonality - decisions based on rules, not personal feelings; (5) written documents and records (files); (6) officials appointed on merit through examinations and qualifications; (7) full-time, salaried career officials with tenure, pensions and promotions based on seniority or merit; and (8) separation of the official from ownership of the means of administration.

Weber considered bureaucracy the most efficient form of organisation for large-scale tasks, but feared that it could become an 'iron cage' that limits freedom. Criticisms: Robert Merton (bureaucratic dysfunctions - 'trained incapacity', goal displacement, rigidity, red tape), Philip Selznick, Alvin Gouldner, Michel Crozier and others pointed to inefficiency, resistance to change, delays and lack of responsiveness. Marxists see bureaucracy as serving the ruling class. Nonetheless, bureaucracy remains the basic structure of modern government, including the Indian civil services.
Organisation is the structured arrangement of people, roles and resources for achieving common objectives.

Organisation is both a structure (the pattern of relationships among positions) and a process (organising activities). L. D. White defined organisation as 'the arrangement of personnel for facilitating the accomplishment of some agreed purpose through the allocation of functions and responsibilities'. Chester Barnard ('The Functions of the Executive', 1938) defined it as 'a system of consciously coordinated activities or forces of two or more persons', requiring communication, willingness to serve and a common purpose.

Types: formal organisation (planned structure, rules, official roles, organisational charts) and informal organisation (social relationships, groups and norms that develop naturally). Principles of organisation include hierarchy (scalar chain), unity of command (one superior for each subordinate), span of control (the number of subordinates one supervisor can manage effectively - Graicunas's formula), delegation, coordination, centralisation and decentralisation, and line and staff agencies. Forms of public organisations include departments, ministries, public corporations (such as the Life Insurance Corporation), independent regulatory commissions, boards and commissions.
Hierarchy arranges offices in levels of authority and responsibility from higher to lower positions.

Hierarchy (scalar principle) means the arrangement of positions in a graded order, like a pyramid, with authority flowing from the top to the bottom and responsibility and communication flowing upward. Henri Fayol described the 'scalar chain' and the 'gangplank' - allowing direct horizontal communication between officials at the same level, with superiors' permission, to avoid delays. In Indian administration, a typical hierarchy is Secretary - Additional Secretary - Joint Secretary - Director - Deputy Secretary - Under Secretary - Section Officer - Assistants.

Merits: clear lines of authority and responsibility, unity of command, coordination, delegation, discipline and channels of communication. Demerits: rigidity, delays and red tape, distortion of communication as it passes through many levels, concentration of power at the top, and discouragement of initiative and creativity at lower levels. Modern organisations use flatter structures, teams and networks to overcome these problems.
Centralisation concentrates decision-making authority at higher levels of an organisation.

Centralisation means the concentration of decision-making authority at the top of an organisation or at the central government. Advantages: uniformity of policies and standards, strong leadership and control, coordination, efficient use of specialised resources, quick decisions in emergencies and national unity. Disadvantages: overload and delays at the top, distance from local conditions and needs, lack of initiative at lower levels, reduced participation and responsiveness, and the risk of authoritarianism.

Factors favouring centralisation include small organisations, national emergencies, the need for uniformity, a lack of competent lower-level personnel and modern communication technology. In India, the Union government's strong powers, central schemes and All-India Services reflect centralising tendencies, while demands for state autonomy and local government reflect pressures for decentralisation.
Decentralisation transfers or distributes authority to lower levels or territorial units.

Decentralisation means the transfer of authority and responsibility from the central level to lower levels or local units. Forms: (1) deconcentration (administrative decentralisation) - transfer of work to field offices of the central government; (2) delegation - transfer of specific powers to semi-autonomous bodies; (3) devolution (political decentralisation) - transfer of powers to elected local governments with their own authority and resources; and (4) privatisation or divestment - transfer of functions to private or non-governmental organisations. Decentralisation may be functional (by subject) or territorial (by area).

Advantages: faster decisions, responsiveness to local needs, people's participation and democracy at the grassroots, reduced burden on the centre, development of local leadership and accountability. Disadvantages: lack of uniformity, coordination problems, inadequate resources and capacity at lower levels, and capture by local elites. In India, the 73rd and 74th Amendments (1992) created a three-tier system of panchayats and municipalities with 29 subjects (Eleventh Schedule) and 18 subjects (Twelfth Schedule), and reserved one-third of seats for women. Mizoram has Village Councils and Autonomous District Councils instead of panchayats.
Leadership is the ability to guide and influence members of an organisation toward common goals.

Leadership is the process of influencing people to work willingly towards organisational goals. Theories: (1) trait theory - leaders have innate qualities such as intelligence, confidence, integrity, initiative and decisiveness ('great man' theory); (2) behavioural theories - focus on what leaders do; the Ohio State and Michigan studies identified task-oriented and people-oriented behaviour; Kurt Lewin's styles - autocratic, democratic and laissez-faire; Blake and Mouton's managerial grid; (3) contingency or situational theories - effective leadership depends on the situation (Fred Fiedler's contingency model; Hersey and Blanchard's situational leadership; House's path-goal theory); and (4) transformational leadership (James MacGregor Burns, Bernard Bass), which inspires followers to go beyond self-interest for a shared vision, versus transactional leadership, based on rewards and punishments.

Functions of administrative leadership: setting goals, planning, organising, motivating, communicating, coordinating, making decisions, representing the organisation and building morale. Chester Barnard emphasised the leader's role in communication and creating cooperation. Good leadership is essential for effective public administration.
Decision-making is the process of selecting a course of action from available alternatives.

Herbert Simon ('Administrative Behaviour', 1947; Nobel Prize in Economics, 1978) argued that decision-making is the heart of administration. He criticised classical 'principles' of administration as 'proverbs' that contradict each other. Steps in rational decision-making: (1) intelligence activity - identifying the problem; (2) design activity - developing alternatives; and (3) choice activity - selecting the best alternative; followed by implementation and review.

Simon introduced 'bounded rationality': because of limited information, time and cognitive ability, administrators cannot find the optimal solution, so they 'satisfice' - choose a satisfactory and sufficient alternative ('administrative man' versus 'economic man'). Charles Lindblom's 'science of muddling through' (1959) described incrementalism - making small, gradual changes from existing policies. Amitai Etzioni proposed 'mixed scanning', combining rational and incremental approaches. Other models include the garbage can model (Cohen, March and Olsen) and group decision-making. Decisions may be programmed (routine) or non-programmed (new and complex).
Administrative accountability means that public officials and agencies are answerable for their actions and use of public authority.

Accountability means that public officials and agencies must answer for their actions, decisions and use of public resources to the people, legislature, courts and higher authorities, and face consequences for misconduct. Types: (1) legislative control - questions, debates, committees (Public Accounts Committee, Estimates Committee, Committee on Public Undertakings), budget approval, no-confidence motions; (2) executive control - ministers, cabinet, civil service rules, budget and audit, appointment and removal; (3) judicial control - judicial review, writs, PIL, administrative tribunals; and (4) popular control - elections, public opinion, media, civil society, citizen charters, social audits, the Right to Information Act (2005), and grievance redressal mechanisms (Centralised Public Grievance Redress and Monitoring System, CPGRAMS).

Other institutions: the Comptroller and Auditor General, the Central Vigilance Commission (1964, statutory since 2003), the Lokpal (Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013; first Lokpal appointed in 2019) and Lokayuktas in states, the Central Bureau of Investigation, and the Ombudsman idea (from Sweden, 1809). Accountability helps prevent corruption, abuse of power and inefficiency.
Recruitment is the process of attracting and selecting suitable personnel for public service.

Recruitment means attracting and selecting suitable candidates for public service. Types: direct recruitment (from outside, through competitive examinations) and indirect recruitment (by promotion from within). In India, recruitment is done by the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC, Article 315-323, originally the Public Service Commission of 1926) for All-India Services (IAS, IPS, IFoS) and central services; State Public Service Commissions (including the Mizoram Public Service Commission) for state services; and the Staff Selection Commission for lower-level posts. The merit-based system was introduced by the Charter Act of 1853 and the Macaulay Committee (1854), based on open competitive examinations.

Methods include written examinations, interviews (personality tests), aptitude tests, group discussions, physical tests and probation. Principles: merit, equal opportunity, transparency and impartiality. Reservations for SCs, STs, OBCs, EWS and persons with disabilities are applied. Lateral entry of specialists at joint secretary and director levels was introduced in 2018, but the 2024 advertisement was withdrawn after criticism about lack of reservation. Issues include delays, coaching-centre culture and the need to test practical skills.
Training develops the knowledge and skills needed by public employees.

Training aims to improve knowledge, skills, attitudes and efficiency of public servants, prepare them for higher responsibilities, keep them updated on new technologies and policies and develop values of integrity and service. Types: pre-entry training (education before joining), post-entry training (after joining), orientation or induction training, in-service training, refresher courses, on-the-job training (learning by working under supervision), and formal training in institutions.

Training institutions in India: the Lal Bahadur Shastri National Academy of Administration (LBSNAA, Mussoorie) for IAS and other services; the Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel National Police Academy (Hyderabad); the Indira Gandhi National Forest Academy (Dehradun); the Indian Institute of Public Administration (New Delhi); and state Administrative Training Institutes (including the Administrative Training Institute in Aizawl). The National Programme for Civil Services Capacity Building - 'Mission Karmayogi' (2020) - aims at competency-based, online training through the iGOT platform.
Promotion advances employees to higher positions according to established rules and criteria.

Promotion means advancement of an employee to a higher post with greater responsibilities, status and pay. It motivates employees, retains talent, rewards experience and merit, and fills higher posts with people familiar with the organisation. Principles: (1) seniority - promotion based on length of service, which is objective and avoids favouritism but may not reward efficiency; (2) merit - based on performance, ability and achievements, assessed through annual performance appraisal reports (APARs), examinations or interviews, which encourages efficiency but may involve subjectivity; and (3) seniority-cum-merit or merit-cum-seniority, combining both.

In India, promotions are decided by Departmental Promotion Committees (DPCs). Reservations in promotion for SCs and STs are allowed under Article 16(4A), subject to conditions laid down by the Supreme Court (M. Nagaraj, 2006 - quantifiable data on backwardness and inadequacy of representation, and efficiency; Jarnail Singh, 2018, removed the requirement of proving backwardness for SCs and STs). Problems include stagnation, delays and litigation.
A budget is an authorised statement of expected public revenue and expenditure for a financial period.

The word 'budget' comes from the French 'bougette', meaning a small leather bag. In India, the Constitution uses the term 'Annual Financial Statement' (Article 112). A budget is a statement of estimated revenues and expenditures of the government for a financial year (1 April to 31 March in India). It is also an instrument of economic policy, planning, accountability and control.

Types: line-item budget (traditional, listing items of expenditure); performance budget (relating expenditure to activities and results, introduced in the USA by the Hoover Commission, 1949, and in India in 1969); planning-programming-budgeting system (PPBS, USA, 1960s); zero-based budgeting (every item justified from zero each year, by Peter Pyhrr; tried in India from 1986); outcome budget (India, 2005, focusing on outcomes); gender budgeting (India, 2005-2006, showing allocations for women); and green budgeting. Budget classification includes revenue and capital budgets, plan and non-plan expenditure (abolished in 2017-2018), and charged and voted expenditure.
Budgeting involves preparation by the executive, legislative consideration and approval, implementation and subsequent financial accountability.

Stages: (1) preparation by the executive - the Ministry of Finance's Budget Division (Department of Economic Affairs) issues a budget circular, ministries submit estimates, the Finance Ministry consults and consolidates, and the Cabinet approves; (2) presentation - the Finance Minister presents the budget in the Lok Sabha (since 2017, on 1 February; the separate Railway Budget was merged into the general budget in 2017); the Economic Survey is presented a day earlier; (3) general discussion in both Houses; (4) scrutiny by Departmentally Related Standing Committees; (5) voting on demands for grants by the Lok Sabha (the Rajya Sabha can only discuss); cut motions (policy cut, economy cut, token cut) may be moved; 'guillotine' applies to remaining demands; (6) passing of the Appropriation Bill (authorising withdrawal from the Consolidated Fund, Article 114) and the Finance Bill (tax proposals, Article 117); and (7) execution and audit.

Other provisions: vote on account (Article 116) allows expenditure for part of the year before the budget is passed, especially in election years; supplementary, additional and excess grants (Article 115); and charged expenditure (such as salaries of the President, judges and the CAG, and debt charges), which is not voted on. Public funds include the Consolidated Fund (Article 266), the Contingency Fund (Article 267) and the Public Account. The Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management Act (2003) sets targets for fiscal deficit. Parliamentary control through the PAC and the CAG ensures accountability.
The CAG is a constitutional authority responsible for auditing public accounts within its constitutional and legal mandate.

The Comptroller and Auditor General of India (Articles 148-151) is appointed by the President for six years or until the age of 65, whichever is earlier, and can be removed only in the manner of a Supreme Court judge. Ambedkar called the CAG the most important officer under the Constitution. The CAG's salary and expenses are charged on the Consolidated Fund; after leaving office, the CAG is not eligible for further government office. The CAG heads the Indian Audit and Accounts Department.

Functions (CAG's Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service Act, 1971): auditing all expenditure from the Consolidated Funds of India and the states, the Contingency Funds and Public Accounts; auditing government companies and corporations; conducting compliance (legality), financial and performance audits (economy, efficiency and effectiveness) and propriety audits; and submitting audit reports to the President (for the Union) and Governors (for states), which are laid before legislatures and examined by the Public Accounts Committee (PAC). The CAG acts as a 'friend, philosopher and guide' of the PAC. Notable reports include those on the 2G spectrum allocation (2010), Commonwealth Games (2011) and coal block allocation (2012). Limitations: post-facto audit only, no power to punish, and audit of secret service expenditure is limited.
The Ministry of Finance plays a central role in fiscal policy, preparation of the Union Budget and management of government finances.

The Ministry of Finance has five departments: the Department of Economic Affairs (which prepares the Union Budget, manages external finance, currency and coinage and capital markets, and publishes the Economic Survey); the Department of Expenditure (public expenditure management, pay commissions, the Office of the Controller General of Accounts); the Department of Revenue (direct and indirect taxes, through the Central Board of Direct Taxes and Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs; GST Council secretariat); the Department of Financial Services (banks, insurance, pensions); and the Department of Investment and Public Asset Management (DIPAM, disinvestment).

Functions: formulating fiscal policy, preparing and implementing the budget, mobilising resources through taxation and borrowing, controlling public expenditure, managing public debt, coordinating with the Reserve Bank of India on monetary and financial matters, administering financial institutions, and representing India in international financial institutions (IMF, World Bank, G20 finance track). The Chief Economic Adviser advises the government. The Finance Commission (Article 280) recommends the sharing of taxes between the Union and states.

sections.title: Public Administration: Meaning, Scope and Significance

blocks.text:
Public administration is concerned with the organisation and implementation of public policies and programmes. It includes administrative organisations, personnel, budgeting, accountability and decision-making.

Modern governments perform extensive social, economic and regulatory functions, so effective administration directly affects citizens and public services.

Public administration is therefore the practical machinery through which governmental objectives are translated into action.

Meaning: public administration is the implementation of public policies through government organisations. Wilson (1887) founded the discipline and proposed the politics-administration dichotomy; White, Gulick, Simon, Waldo and Appleby offered definitions emphasising management, policy implementation and public character. Public and private administration share techniques but differ in purpose, accountability, legal framework and scale.

Scope: POSDCORB view (Gulick) of managerial functions; the subject-matter view (functions of departments such as defence, education, health); integral and managerial views; and modern scope including organisation, personnel, finance, policy, local government, development administration, accountability, governance and e-governance. Evolution: classical theories (Taylor, Fayol, Weber), human relations (Mayo), behavioural approach (Simon), systems and ecological approaches (Fred Riggs), New Public Administration (1968), New Public Management (1980s-1990s) and governance.

Significance: implementation of laws and policies, service delivery, law and order, development and welfare, crisis management, continuity and stability, and nation-building in developing countries. In India, administrative reforms include the Administrative Reforms Commissions (1966, 2005), RTI, citizens' charters, e-governance, direct benefit transfers and Mission Karmayogi. Effective administration is essential for good governance.

sections.title: Scientific Management, Human Relations and Bureaucratic Approaches

blocks.text:
Scientific management emphasises efficiency, specialisation and systematic organisation of work. The human relations approach draws attention to motivation, informal groups and the social side of organisations.

The bureaucratic approach focuses on formal hierarchy, rules, specialised offices and impersonal administration.

Each approach highlights a different dimension of administration: efficiency, human behaviour and formal organisational structure.

Scientific management (Taylor, 1911): one best way of doing work; time-and-motion studies; scientific selection and training; division of responsibility between management and workers; incentive wages; contributions - efficiency, standardisation and systematic management; criticisms - treats workers as machines, ignores human factors, causes monotony and alienation. Related classical theories include Fayol's 14 principles and Gulick's POSDCORB.

Human relations approach (Mayo, Hawthorne experiments, 1924-1932): workers are social beings; informal groups, morale, communication, participation and supervision influence productivity; the organisation is a social system; non-economic rewards matter. Later behavioural theories (Maslow, McGregor, Herzberg) developed motivation theory. Criticisms: overemphasis on informal relations and human factors, neglect of structure and economic incentives, possible manipulation.

Bureaucratic approach (Weber): an ideal type based on legal-rational authority - hierarchy, specialisation, rules, impersonality, written records, merit recruitment, salaried career officials; considered the most efficient and rational form for large organisations. Criticisms: dysfunctions such as red tape, rigidity, goal displacement and lack of responsiveness (Merton); the danger of the 'iron cage'. Comparison: scientific management focuses on efficiency of work, human relations on people and their needs, and bureaucracy on formal structure and rules; each highlights a different dimension, and modern administration combines insights from all three.

Organisation coordinates people and roles for common objectives. Hierarchy establishes levels of authority and responsibility.

Centralisation places major decision-making at higher levels, which may promote uniformity and control. Decentralisation distributes authority downward or territorially, which may improve responsiveness and participation.

Administrative systems normally combine these principles rather than relying entirely on one form.

Organisation: a structure and process of coordinating people and activities for common goals (White, Barnard); formal and informal organisation; principles such as hierarchy, unity of command, span of control, delegation, coordination, line and staff. Types of public organisations: departments, public corporations, independent regulatory commissions, boards and autonomous bodies.

Hierarchy: graded levels of authority with a scalar chain (Fayol); it provides clear authority, responsibility, communication channels and discipline, but can cause rigidity, delays, communication distortion and centralisation. Centralisation: concentration of authority at the top; advantages - uniformity, control, coordination, efficiency in emergencies; disadvantages - delays, overload, distance from local needs, lack of initiative and participation.

Decentralisation: transfer of authority to lower levels or local governments - deconcentration, delegation, devolution and privatisation; advantages - quick decisions, responsiveness, participation, local leadership, accountability; disadvantages - lack of uniformity, coordination problems, inadequate capacity and resources, local elite capture. India's panchayati raj (73rd and 74th Amendments) and Mizoram's Village Councils and ADCs are examples of decentralisation. Effective administration requires a balance - centralisation of policy-making and decentralisation of implementation, depending on the size, nature and environment of the organisation.

Leadership guides people and influences organisational behaviour. Decision-making involves choosing among alternative courses of action and is a central function of administration.

Accountability requires public officials to explain and justify their actions and allows institutions to review the use of public authority.

Good administration therefore requires not only efficient decisions but also responsible and answerable exercise of power.

Leadership: influencing people towards goals; theories - trait, behavioural (autocratic, democratic, laissez-faire; managerial grid), contingency (Fiedler, Hersey-Blanchard, path-goal) and transformational versus transactional leadership. Functions - goal-setting, planning, organising, motivating, communicating, coordinating, decision-making and representing. Effective leaders build morale, adapt to situations and act with integrity.

Decision-making: the core of administration (Simon); stages - intelligence, design and choice; bounded rationality and 'satisficing'; incrementalism (Lindblom's 'muddling through'); mixed scanning (Etzioni); programmed and non-programmed decisions; individual and group decisions. Good decisions require information, analysis, consultation and consideration of consequences, including ethical and social effects.

Accountability: answerability for actions and use of resources; legislative control (questions, committees, budget), executive control (hierarchy, rules, audit), judicial control (judicial review, writs, tribunals) and popular control (elections, media, RTI, social audit, citizen charters, grievance redressal); institutions - CAG, CVC, Lokpal and Lokayuktas, CBI. Good administration combines effective leadership and sound decisions with responsible and answerable use of power, protecting citizens from arbitrary action and corruption.

sections.title: Personnel Administration: Recruitment, Training and Promotion

blocks.text:
Personnel administration manages the human resources of government. Recruitment brings suitable individuals into public service. Training develops their skills and administrative competence.

Promotion provides advancement and can encourage experience, performance and career development when governed by fair procedures.

The quality of public administration depends greatly on a competent and professionally managed public service.

Personnel administration (human resource management) includes recruitment, classification of posts, pay and service conditions, training, promotion, discipline, morale, performance appraisal, employee welfare, retirement benefits and relations between employees and government. In India, the civil services are classified into All-India Services (IAS, IPS, IFoS - Article 312), Central Services (Group A, B, C, D, such as IFS, IRS) and State Services. Constitutional provisions include Articles 308-323 (services and public service commissions) and Article 311 (safeguards against dismissal or removal of civil servants).

Recruitment: merit-based through the UPSC, State PSCs and SSC, with examinations and interviews, reservations, and recent lateral entry; issues - delays, the need for skill-based recruitment and diversity. Training: pre-entry, induction, in-service, on-the-job and refresher training; institutions - LBSNAA, SVPNPA, IIPA, state ATIs; reforms - Mission Karmayogi (competency-based, digital learning). Promotion: by seniority, merit or a combination, decided by DPCs; reservation in promotion under Article 16(4A) with judicial conditions; problems - stagnation, subjectivity and litigation.

Reforms recommended by the Second Administrative Reforms Commission (2005-2009, 'Refurbishing of Personnel Administration', 10th report) include performance-based assessment, mid-career training, domain expertise, fixed tenure for key posts, protection from arbitrary transfers, and a code of ethics. A competent, motivated, professional and ethical civil service is essential for good governance.

The budget presents expected public revenue and expenditure and must pass through constitutional and legislative procedures. The executive prepares the budget, while Parliament considers and authorises public expenditure.

The Ministry of Finance has a central role in fiscal management and Union budgeting. The Comptroller and Auditor General audits public accounts within its constitutional mandate and strengthens financial accountability.

Budgeting and audit therefore connect public spending with legislative control and accountability.

Budget: a statement of estimated revenue and expenditure (the Annual Financial Statement, Article 112) and an instrument of economic policy and accountability; types include line-item, performance, PPBS, zero-based, outcome and gender budgets. Budget process in India: preparation by the Finance Ministry with ministries; approval by the Cabinet; presentation in Parliament on 1 February; general discussion; scrutiny by standing committees; voting on demands for grants (Lok Sabha only), with cut motions and guillotine; passing of the Appropriation Bill and Finance Bill; vote on account; supplementary grants; execution and audit. Charged expenditure is not voted. The FRBM Act sets fiscal discipline targets.

Finance Ministry: departments of Economic Affairs, Expenditure, Revenue, Financial Services and DIPAM; functions - fiscal policy, budget preparation, taxation, expenditure control, public debt management, financial sector regulation in coordination with the RBI, and international economic relations. CAG: constitutional authority (Articles 148-151) independent of the executive; audits government accounts and public sector undertakings (compliance, financial and performance audits); reports to the President or Governors, examined by the PAC; limitations - post-facto audit and lack of enforcement powers.

Financial accountability chain: the executive prepares and implements the budget; Parliament authorises expenditure and taxation ('no taxation without representation'); the CAG audits; the PAC and other committees examine reports and recommend action. This system links public spending with legislative control and accountability, essential for preventing waste and corruption.
Political sociology studies the relationship between society and politics, including how social structures affect political power and behaviour.

Political sociology is an interdisciplinary field between political science and sociology. Lipset and Bendix defined it as the study of 'the social bases of politics'; Giovanni Sartori distinguished 'sociology of politics' (explaining politics through social factors) from 'political sociology' (a genuine interdisciplinary approach studying the interaction between social and political structures). Its founders include Karl Marx (class and politics), Max Weber (authority, bureaucracy, stratification), Émile Durkheim (social solidarity), Vilfredo Pareto, Gaetano Mosca and Robert Michels (elite theory), and later Seymour Martin Lipset ('Political Man', 1960), Gabriel Almond and Sidney Verba ('The Civic Culture', 1963), Reinhard Bendix and Barrington Moore ('Social Origins of Dictatorship and Democracy', 1966).

It studies how social factors - class, caste, religion, ethnicity, gender, education, family and culture - affect political behaviour, institutions and power, and how political institutions in turn shape society.
The field developed from growing interest in the social foundations of political institutions and behaviour.

Political sociology emerged in the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries from the work of Marx, Weber, Durkheim and the elite theorists, who studied the social foundations of political power. It developed as a distinct field after the Second World War, especially in the USA, influenced by the behavioural revolution, which shifted attention from formal institutions to political behaviour, and by the need to understand fascism, communism, democracy and the politics of newly independent countries.

Factors: the inadequacy of the legal-institutional approach; the growth of empirical social research (surveys, voting studies such as Paul Lazarsfeld's 'The People's Choice', 1944); interest in political development and modernisation in the Third World; and the interdisciplinary trend in social sciences. In India, scholars such as Rajni Kothari, M. N. Srinivas (dominant caste, Sanskritisation), Andre Béteille, Rudolph and Rudolph, and Yogendra Yadav (election studies) contributed to political sociology.
Its scope includes power, authority, legitimacy, political culture, socialisation, participation, stratification, caste and politics.

Nature: political sociology is interdisciplinary, empirical and behavioural (using observation, surveys and quantitative methods), but also theoretical and historical. It focuses on processes and relationships rather than only formal institutions. It studies both the influence of society on politics and the influence of politics on society.

Scope: (1) power, authority and legitimacy; (2) political culture and socialisation; (3) political participation, voting behaviour and public opinion; (4) political parties, pressure groups and social movements; (5) elites and leadership; (6) social stratification - class, caste, race, gender - and their political effects; (7) bureaucracy; (8) political development and modernisation; (9) political change, revolution and conflict; (10) nationalism, ethnicity and identity politics; and (11) political communication and media. In India, important themes include caste and politics, religion and politics, regionalism, tribal politics and social movements.
This approach studies political structures by examining the functions they perform for the political system.

Structural-functionalism, developed in sociology by Talcott Parsons and Robert Merton and in anthropology by Malinowski and Radcliffe-Brown, was applied to politics by Gabriel Almond ('The Politics of the Developing Areas', 1960, with James Coleman; 'Comparative Politics: A Developmental Approach', 1966, with G. Bingham Powell). It asks what functions are performed in a political system and which structures perform them. Every political system performs certain functions, though structures differ across countries.

Almond identified input functions - political socialisation and recruitment, interest articulation (by pressure groups), interest aggregation (by parties), and political communication - and output functions - rule-making (legislature), rule application (executive) and rule adjudication (judiciary). Later he added system capabilities (extractive, regulative, distributive, symbolic, responsive) and conversion, adaptation and maintenance functions. Merton distinguished manifest and latent functions and dysfunctions. Criticisms: it is conservative (focuses on stability and equilibrium), static, vague, Western-centric and does not explain change or conflict well.
Systems analysis views politics as an interconnected system that receives demands and support and produces authoritative decisions.

David Easton ('The Political System', 1953; 'A Framework for Political Analysis', 1965; 'A Systems Analysis of Political Life', 1965) introduced systems analysis into political science. He defined politics as the 'authoritative allocation of values for a society' and the political system as the set of interactions through which this occurs. The system exists in an environment (intra-societal - economy, culture, social structure; and extra-societal - international system).

The system receives inputs - demands (for goods, services, regulations, participation) and supports (obedience, taxes, voting, loyalty) - and converts them through the 'black box' of decision-making into outputs - authoritative decisions and policies (laws, regulations, allocation of resources). Outputs produce outcomes that affect the environment and generate feedback, leading to new demands and supports. 'Gatekeepers' (parties, pressure groups, media) regulate the flow of demands to prevent overload. The system seeks to persist through adaptation. Criticisms: abstract and difficult to test empirically; emphasises stability and equilibrium; neglects power, conflict, history and the role of individuals; and the 'black box' of conversion processes is not explained fully. Karl Deutsch's communications approach ('The Nerves of Government', 1963) is related.
Power is the capacity to influence behaviour, decisions or outcomes.

Max Weber defined power as the probability that one actor will be able to carry out his own will despite resistance. Robert Dahl defined it as A's ability to get B to do something B would not otherwise do. Bertrand Russell defined power as 'the production of intended effects'. Talcott Parsons saw power as a generalised capacity to get things done for collective goals ('power to', not only 'power over').

Steven Lukes's three faces of power: (1) the decision-making face - who prevails in observable conflicts (Dahl, pluralists); (2) the non-decision-making face - the ability to keep issues off the agenda (Bachrach and Baratz, 1962); and (3) the ideological face - shaping people's preferences, so they accept their situation (Lukes, influenced by Gramsci's hegemony). Michel Foucault saw power as dispersed throughout society, embedded in knowledge, discourses, institutions (prisons, hospitals, schools) and everyday practices - 'power is everywhere' - and as productive, not only repressive.
Power may operate through coercion, economic resources, political position, persuasion or other forms of influence.

Kinds of power: (1) political power - exercised by the state and government through laws and policies; (2) economic power - control over wealth, resources and production (Marx saw it as the basis of political power); (3) military or coercive power - the use or threat of force; (4) ideological or cultural power - shaping beliefs and values through religion, education and media; (5) social power - status and influence in society (caste, family, community); and (6) personal power - charisma and expertise.

French and Raven (1959) identified five bases of social power: legitimate power (based on position), reward power, coercive power, expert power and referent power (identification with and admiration for a person); later they added informational power. Michael Mann ('The Sources of Social Power') identified four sources - ideological, economic, military and political (IEMP model). Joseph Nye distinguished hard power (coercion and payment) and soft power (attraction). Power can be legitimate (authority) or illegitimate (coercion).
Elite theory argues that a relatively small group exercises disproportionate political influence.

Classical elite theorists: Vilfredo Pareto ('The Mind and Society', 1916) argued that every society is divided into a governing elite, a non-governing elite and the masses; elites are superior in ability and rule through force ('lions') or cunning ('foxes'), and history is a 'graveyard of aristocracies' because elites decline and are replaced ('circulation of elites'). Gaetano Mosca ('The Ruling Class', 1896) argued that an organised minority always rules over the disorganised majority. Robert Michels ('Political Parties', 1911) proposed the 'iron law of oligarchy' - 'who says organisation says oligarchy' - showing that even democratic socialist parties become dominated by a small leadership.

Modern elite theory: C. Wright Mills ('The Power Elite', 1956) argued that in the USA, power is concentrated in a 'power elite' of top corporate executives, military leaders and political leaders who share similar backgrounds and interests. Joseph Schumpeter's 'democratic elitism' accepted that elites rule but argued that democracy means competition among elites for votes. Elite theory challenges classical democratic theory and Marxism (which sees power based on class). Criticisms: it is anti-democratic, assumes that the masses are incapable, and underestimates the influence of elections, groups and social movements.
Pluralism sees power as dispersed among many competing groups rather than permanently monopolised by one elite.

Pluralism argues that in liberal democracies, power is dispersed among many groups - business, labour, professional associations, religious groups, ethnic groups, consumer and environmental groups - which compete and bargain to influence policy. No single group dominates permanently; different groups win on different issues. The government acts as a referee or arena. Arthur Bentley ('The Process of Government', 1908) and David Truman ('The Governmental Process', 1951) developed group theory.

Robert Dahl's 'Who Governs?' (1961), a study of New Haven, Connecticut, found that different groups and leaders influenced different issues (education, urban redevelopment, party nominations), concluding that power was dispersed. He described modern democracies as 'polyarchies' - rule by many, with competition and participation. Critics: elite theorists (Mills) and Marxists argued that groups have unequal resources and access, and business has a privileged position (Charles Lindblom's 'neo-pluralism', 'Politics and Markets', 1977); Bachrach and Baratz argued that pluralists ignore 'non-decisions'. Pluralism remains influential in explaining interest-group politics.
The Marxian approach connects political power with class relations and control over economic resources.

Marxists argue that political power derives from economic power: the class that owns the means of production (the bourgeoisie in capitalism) controls the state, which is 'a committee for managing the common affairs of the whole bourgeoisie'. Power is therefore structural and concentrated in the ruling class, and political conflicts reflect class struggle. Ideology (religion, culture, media, education) legitimises this domination, creating 'false consciousness' among workers.

Later Marxists developed the theory: Antonio Gramsci argued that the ruling class maintains power through 'hegemony' - cultural and ideological leadership that wins the consent of the masses through civil society institutions (church, schools, media), not only through coercion; Ralph Miliband ('The State in Capitalist Society', 1969) emphasised the common background and connections between state elites and capitalists (instrumentalism); Nicos Poulantzas emphasised the structural constraints that make the state serve capitalism even without direct control ('relative autonomy'). Criticisms: economic determinism, neglect of other sources of power (bureaucracy, military, ideology, gender, race), and the experience of communist states where a new political elite dominated (Milovan Djilas's 'The New Class', 1957).
Authority is power regarded as rightful or legitimate.

Authority is legitimate power - power accepted as rightful by those subject to it. It is based on consent rather than coercion. Robert Bierstedt described authority as 'institutionalised power'. Elements of authority include legitimacy, a recognised right to command, an obligation to obey, and institutional backing.

Authority differs from power (the capacity to influence, which may be coercive) and from influence (persuasion without the right to command). Authority makes compliance easier and less costly, contributes to stability and is essential for government. It can be political, legal, religious, administrative or traditional. Limits of authority include laws, constitutions, moral norms and public opinion; when authority is abused or loses legitimacy, people may resist through protests, civil disobedience or revolution.
A common sociological classification distinguishes traditional, charismatic and legal-rational authority.

Max Weber classified authority into three ideal types: (1) traditional authority - based on belief in the sanctity of long-standing traditions and customs; obedience is owed to persons who occupy positions by tradition, such as hereditary monarchs, tribal chiefs (the Mizo lal) and patriarchs; it may be patrimonial or feudal; (2) charismatic authority - based on devotion to the extraordinary personal qualities, heroism or sanctity of an individual leader, such as prophets, religious leaders, revolutionary leaders (Gandhi, Napoleon, Lenin, Mao); it is unstable and must be 'routinised' into traditional or legal forms after the leader's death; and (3) legal-rational authority - based on belief in the legality of rules and the right of those in office under these rules to issue commands; obedience is owed to the office, not the person, as in modern bureaucracies and constitutional governments.

In reality, authority often combines types - for example, a democratically elected leader may have legal-rational authority and charisma. Weber saw modern society moving towards legal-rational authority with the growth of bureaucracy.
Legitimacy is the belief that political authority is rightful and deserves acceptance.

Legitimacy is the belief that a political system, its institutions and rulers have a rightful claim to obedience. Seymour Martin Lipset said legitimacy involves 'the capacity of the system to engender and maintain the belief that the existing political institutions are the most appropriate ones for the society'. David Beetham ('The Legitimation of Power', 1991) argued that power is legitimate when it conforms to established rules, the rules are justified by shared beliefs, and there is evidence of consent.

A legitimacy crisis occurs when people lose faith in the system, which may lead to instability, protests, revolutions or coups (Jürgen Habermas's 'Legitimation Crisis', 1973, argued that capitalist democracies face crises when they cannot meet expectations). Legitimacy is crucial because no government can rule for long by force alone; voluntary compliance reduces the costs of government.
Legitimacy may arise from tradition, law, institutions, leadership, performance or accepted political values.

Sources of legitimacy: (1) tradition and custom (monarchy, chieftainship); (2) charisma of leaders; (3) legality - rule according to the constitution and law; (4) democratic elections and consent of the governed; (5) ideology - nationalism, communism, religion (theocracy); (6) performance - economic growth, welfare, security and good governance (sometimes called 'output legitimacy' or 'performance legitimacy', as claimed by the Chinese government); (7) procedural fairness and accountability; and (8) international recognition.

In India, the legitimacy of the state rests on the Constitution, democratic elections, the legacy of the freedom struggle, rule of law, protection of rights and welfare policies. Threats to legitimacy include corruption, inefficiency, inequality, violence, communal conflict and perceived injustice. In Mizoram, the legitimacy of the political system was strengthened by the Peace Accord, statehood, constitutional protection under Article 371G and the participation of civil society.
Political culture refers to orientations, values and attitudes toward politics and political institutions.

Gabriel Almond and Sidney Verba ('The Civic Culture', 1963) defined political culture as 'the specifically political orientations - attitudes toward the political system and its various parts, and attitudes toward the role of the self in the system'. Lucian Pye defined it as 'the set of attitudes, beliefs and sentiments which give order and meaning to a political process'. Political culture is shaped by history, religion, social structure, education, economic development and political experience.

Almond and Verba identified three types of orientations: cognitive (knowledge and beliefs about the political system), affective (feelings of attachment, involvement or rejection) and evaluative (judgements and opinions). Political culture includes national identity, attitudes to authority, trust in institutions, tolerance, participation and beliefs about rights. It influences the stability and functioning of democracy - for example, whether citizens trust institutions, participate and accept election results.
Political culture may be classified into different types according to levels and forms of citizen orientation and participation.

Almond and Verba's typology, based on surveys in five countries (USA, UK, West Germany, Italy and Mexico): (1) parochial political culture - citizens have little awareness of or interest in the national political system; they are oriented to local communities (found in traditional and tribal societies); (2) subject political culture - citizens are aware of the political system and its outputs but see themselves as passive subjects who obey rather than participate (as in authoritarian regimes; they found elements in Germany and Italy); and (3) participant political culture - citizens are aware of both inputs and outputs and actively participate in politics (found in democratic societies).

They argued that the 'civic culture', a mixed culture combining participant orientations with subject and parochial elements (allowing participation while maintaining stability and trust), was most suitable for stable democracy, as in Britain and the USA. Criticisms: the typology is Western-centric, static and does not explain how culture changes; it treats culture as the cause of political outcomes rather than also as a result. Other typologies include Daniel Elazar's moralistic, individualistic and traditionalistic cultures (in US states) and Ronald Inglehart's post-materialism. Indian political culture is often described as a mix - highly participatory in elections but with strong elements of deference, caste and community loyalty.
Political socialisation is the process through which people acquire political values, attitudes and orientations.

Political socialisation is the process by which individuals learn political values, attitudes, beliefs and behaviour, and by which political culture is transmitted from one generation to the next. Herbert Hyman ('Political Socialization', 1959) introduced the term. It is a lifelong process, but childhood and adolescence are particularly important; early learning is often more durable (David Easton and Robert Hess's studies on children's attitudes to authority).

Socialisation can be direct (explicit teaching of political information and values, as in civics education) or indirect (learning through experiences, family relationships and observation). It can be manifest or latent. Socialisation contributes to political stability by creating support for the system, but can also produce change when new generations develop different values (for example, through social movements). Totalitarian states use intense propaganda and youth organisations for political socialisation.
Family, school, peer groups, media, political institutions and social organisations can act as agents of political socialisation.

Agents: (1) family - the first and most important agent; children often adopt their parents' party identification, religious views and attitudes to authority; (2) school and education - civics curriculum, textbooks, national rituals (flag hoisting, anthem, national days), teachers and student politics; (3) peer groups - friends and colleagues influence attitudes, especially among young people; (4) mass media - newspapers, television, radio, cinema and increasingly social media (Facebook, WhatsApp, YouTube, X), which shape political knowledge and opinion, sometimes spreading misinformation; (5) religious institutions - churches, temples and mosques influence values; (6) political parties and leaders - through campaigns and propaganda; (7) workplace and trade unions; (8) social and community organisations; and (9) political events and experiences (wars, movements, elections).

In Mizoram, important agents include the family, schools, churches (Sunday schools, youth fellowships), the YMA, MZP, MHIP and the media, which shape strong community values and political awareness. Social media has become increasingly influential among youth everywhere.
Political participation means involvement by citizens in political activities and public decision-making.

Political participation includes all voluntary activities through which citizens try to influence the selection of rulers and public policies. Verba and Nie ('Participation in America', 1972) identified modes such as voting, campaign activity, communal activity (working with others to solve community problems) and particularised contacts with officials. Lester Milbrath ('Political Participation', 1965) described a hierarchy: spectator activities (voting, discussing politics, wearing badges), transitional activities (attending meetings, contributing money) and gladiatorial activities (holding office, being a candidate, party leadership), noting that only a small percentage engage in the highest activities.

Factors affecting participation: education, income and social class, age, gender, caste, urban or rural residence, political interest and efficacy, party and group membership, media exposure and political culture. In India, voter turnout has been high, especially among rural voters, women (women's turnout exceeded men's in several elections) and the poor, unlike in many Western democracies where the educated and wealthy participate more - Yogendra Yadav called this the 'second democratic upsurge'. Low participation can result from apathy, alienation or barriers, while high participation may indicate engagement or mobilisation.
Voting, campaigning, party activity, public meetings, petitions and protest are examples of political participation.

Conventional forms: voting in elections; campaigning for candidates or parties; joining a party and party work; contacting representatives and officials; attending public meetings; signing petitions; membership of pressure groups and civil society organisations; participation in local government (gram sabhas, village councils); and contesting elections. Unconventional forms: protests, demonstrations, marches, strikes, boycotts, sit-ins (dharnas), hunger strikes, civil disobedience, social movements and, in extreme cases, political violence.

New forms include online participation (social media campaigns, online petitions, hashtag activism), consumer activism, participatory budgeting and public consultations. Examples in India include the Anna Hazare anti-corruption movement (2011), the Nirbhaya protests (2012), farmers' protests against farm laws (2020-2021, which led to repeal of the laws) and the anti-CAA protests (2019-2020). In Mizoram, participation includes high voter turnout and active involvement in civil society organisations.
Social stratification is the structured inequality and ranking of groups within society.

Social stratification is the hierarchical arrangement of individuals and groups in society based on unequal access to wealth, power, status and prestige. It is a characteristic of society, not merely individual differences; it persists over generations; it is universal but variable in form; and it is supported by beliefs that justify inequality (Melvin Tumin).

Forms of stratification: slavery (ownership of people), estate (feudal Europe - clergy, nobility, commoners), caste (hereditary, endogamous groups ranked by ritual purity, as in India), and class (based on economic position, more open, with possible mobility). Theories: the functionalist theory (Kingsley Davis and Wilbert Moore, 1945) argues that stratification is necessary to motivate talented people to fill important positions; the conflict theory (Marx) argues that stratification results from exploitation and serves the interests of the dominant class; and Weber's multidimensional theory distinguishes class (economic), status (social honour) and party (political power).
It involves differentiated social positions, unequal rewards and relatively persistent patterns of hierarchy.

Elements: (1) differentiation - society is divided into different positions and roles; (2) ranking - positions are ranked according to their importance, prestige or value; (3) evaluation - members of society evaluate and judge these positions as superior or inferior; and (4) rewarding - positions receive unequal rewards (income, wealth, power, prestige, privileges and life chances). Inequalities are institutionalised and persistent.

Dimensions of stratification (Weber): class (economic position in the market), status (social honour, lifestyle, prestige - for example, caste or educational status) and party (political power and organisation). Social mobility - the movement of individuals or groups between positions - can be vertical (upward or downward) or horizontal, intra-generational or inter-generational. Open systems (class) allow more mobility than closed systems (caste, estate).
Indian stratification has been shaped by caste, class, gender and other social divisions.

Caste: the most distinctive form of stratification in India, based on the varna model (Brahmana, Kshatriya, Vaishya, Shudra, with 'untouchables' outside) and thousands of jatis; characteristics include birth-based membership, endogamy, hierarchy based on purity and pollution, restrictions on food and social interaction, hereditary occupations and caste councils. Louis Dumont ('Homo Hierarchicus', 1966) emphasised the principle of purity and pollution. M. N. Srinivas described 'Sanskritisation' (lower castes adopting upper-caste customs to rise in status) and 'dominant caste' (a caste that is numerically strong, economically and politically powerful in a region).

Class: modern economic changes have created classes based on occupation, income and education - landlords, rich peasants, agricultural labourers, industrial workers, the middle class and business classes - which often overlap with caste. Gender: women have been subordinated through patriarchy, with limited property rights, education and political participation. Other dimensions include religion, tribe, region and language. In tribal societies such as Mizoram, caste does not exist, but stratification historically existed between chiefs, commoners and bawi; today it is based on class, education, occupation and gender. Constitutional measures (Articles 15-17, reservations) and social movements have aimed to reduce caste and gender inequalities.
Caste can influence political identity, mobilisation, leadership and voting, while democratic politics can also transform caste relationships.

Rajni Kothari argued that caste has become politicised: caste associations have become political actors, parties mobilise caste groups, candidates are selected according to caste arithmetic, and caste influences voting behaviour. At the same time, democracy has changed caste - it has given lower castes a voice and power through numbers, weakened the ritual hierarchy and created caste coalitions. Lloyd and Susanne Rudolph described how caste associations became vehicles of democratisation ('The Modernity of Tradition', 1967). M. N. Srinivas's concept of the 'dominant caste' explains local power structures.

Major developments: the rise of the OBCs after the Mandal Commission (implemented in 1990); the Dalit assertion through the BSP (Kanshi Ram, Mayawati) and other movements; caste-based parties and leaders (SP, RJD); and the BJP's efforts to build broad caste coalitions under Hindutva. Christophe Jaffrelot called this India's 'silent revolution' - the rise of lower castes in north Indian politics. Debates include the caste census (Bihar's caste survey, 2023, and the central government's decision in 2025 to include caste in the next census), sub-categorisation of OBCs and SCs, and the persistence of caste violence. Caste and politics thus influence each other.

sections.title: Political Sociology: Meaning, Nature, Emergence and Scope

blocks.text:
Political sociology studies the interaction between political institutions and social structures. It asks how society shapes political power and how politics in turn changes social relations.

Its scope includes power, authority, legitimacy, political culture, political socialisation, participation, social stratification and caste. The field emerged from the recognition that political institutions cannot be fully understood separately from society.

Political sociology therefore forms an important bridge between Political Science and Sociology.

Meaning and nature: political sociology studies the social bases of politics and the interaction between society and politics (Lipset, Bendix, Sartori). It is interdisciplinary, empirical, behavioural, comparative and process-oriented. Emergence: rooted in Marx, Weber, Durkheim, Pareto, Mosca and Michels; developed as a field after the Second World War with the behavioural revolution, voting studies and the study of political development; in India, scholars like Rajni Kothari, M. N. Srinivas and Yogendra Yadav contributed.

Scope: power, authority and legitimacy; political culture and socialisation; participation and voting behaviour; parties, pressure groups and social movements; elites and leadership; social stratification (class, caste, gender, race); bureaucracy; nationalism, ethnicity and identity politics; political development and change; and political communication. In India, issues such as caste, religion, regionalism, tribal identity, gender and social movements are central.

Significance: political sociology shows that political institutions cannot be understood separately from the social structures in which they operate - for example, why democracy functions differently in different societies, how caste affects elections, and how social movements change policies. It bridges political science and sociology and helps explain both stability and change.

Structural-functional analysis studies political structures according to the functions they perform. Institutions are examined as parts of a wider political system whose activities contribute to system operation.

Systems analysis also treats politics as an interconnected whole. Demands and support enter the political system and authoritative decisions emerge as outputs, with feedback affecting later processes.

Both approaches move beyond the study of formal constitutions to analyse political processes and relationships.

Structural-functional analysis (Almond, Powell, Coleman): every political system performs certain functions through different structures; input functions - socialisation and recruitment, interest articulation, interest aggregation, political communication; output functions - rule-making, rule application, rule adjudication; system capabilities - extractive, regulative, distributive, symbolic and responsive. Merton's concepts of manifest and latent functions and dysfunctions add depth. It allows comparison of different political systems, including non-Western ones, by focusing on functions rather than formal institutions.

Systems analysis (Easton): the political system as a set of interactions that authoritatively allocate values; inputs (demands and supports) from the environment are converted into outputs (decisions and policies), with feedback; gatekeepers regulate demands; the system seeks persistence through adaptation. Related approaches include Karl Deutsch's communications theory.

Evaluation: both approaches moved political science beyond legal and institutional studies, introduced a holistic and comparative perspective, and influenced the study of developing countries. Criticisms: they emphasise stability, equilibrium and system maintenance, neglecting conflict, power and change; they are abstract, difficult to test and Western-centric; and they treat the political system as a 'black box'. Despite these limitations, their concepts (inputs, outputs, feedback, functions) remain useful in analysing politics.

sections.title: Power: Elite, Pluralist and Marxian Theories

blocks.text:
Elite theory argues that political influence is concentrated in the hands of a relatively small group. Pluralist theory disagrees with the idea of permanent concentration and sees multiple groups competing for influence.

The Marxian theory links political power to class relations and control over economic resources. It emphasises structural inequality and conflict between classes.

These theories offer different answers to the question: who actually holds power in society?

Elite theory: classical elite theorists (Pareto - circulation of elites; Mosca - ruling class; Michels - iron law of oligarchy) argued that a minority always rules; C. Wright Mills described the 'power elite' of corporate, military and political leaders in the USA; Schumpeter's democratic elitism accepted elite competition as the essence of democracy. Strengths: realistic analysis of concentrated power; weaknesses: anti-democratic assumptions and neglect of mass influence.
