Pluralist theory: power is dispersed among many competing groups; no single group dominates (Bentley, Truman, Dahl's 'Who Governs?', polyarchy); the state is a neutral arena or referee. Criticisms: groups have unequal resources; business has a privileged position (Lindblom's neo-pluralism); 'non-decisions' and agenda-setting are ignored (Bachrach and Baratz); and many people are not organised in groups. Marxian theory: power is based on class and ownership of the means of production; the state serves the ruling class (instrumental and structural views - Miliband, Poulantzas); hegemony (Gramsci) secures consent. Criticisms: economic determinism and neglect of other sources of power.

Comparison and evaluation: the three theories answer the question 'Who holds power?' differently - a minority elite, many competing groups, or the economic ruling class. Each captures part of reality: elite theory explains concentration of power in leadership, pluralism explains group bargaining in democracies, and Marxism explains the influence of economic structures. Lukes's three dimensions and Foucault's diffuse power provide additional perspectives. In India, all three can be applied - political dynasties and elites, competition among caste and interest groups, and the influence of business on policy.

Authority is power accepted as rightful. It differs from mere coercion because people recognise a claim to rule. Traditional, charismatic and legal-rational authority are important sociological types.

Legitimacy is the wider belief that institutions or rulers have a valid right to exercise authority. It may rest on law, tradition, leadership, performance or accepted political values.

Stable political systems normally depend on legitimacy as well as power.

Authority: legitimate power, accepted as rightful; differs from coercion and influence; Weber's three types - traditional (custom and heredity, such as monarchs and tribal chiefs), charismatic (extraordinary personal qualities, such as Gandhi; unstable and requiring routinisation) and legal-rational (rules and offices, such as modern bureaucracies and constitutional governments). Modern societies are dominated by legal-rational authority, though charisma remains important in politics.

Legitimacy: the belief that authority is rightful (Lipset, Beetham); sources - tradition, charisma, legality, elections and consent, ideology, performance and international recognition; legitimacy crises arise when governments fail to meet expectations or violate norms (Habermas). Legitimacy reduces the need for coercion, ensures voluntary compliance, and provides stability.

Relationship: power + legitimacy = authority. Stable political systems depend on legitimacy as well as power. For example, democratic governments derive legitimacy from free elections and constitutional rule, while authoritarian regimes may rely on performance, ideology or nationalism, and resort to force when legitimacy declines. In Mizoram, the transition from traditional authority (chiefs) to legal-rational authority (elected councils and the state government), and the restoration of legitimacy after the Peace Accord, illustrate these concepts.

Political culture consists of values and orientations toward political institutions and processes. Political socialisation is the process through which such orientations are learned.

Family, schools, media, peer groups and political institutions can act as agents of socialisation. Political participation includes voting, campaigning, party activity, petitions and protest.

Together these concepts explain how citizens become connected to political life.

Political culture: the attitudes, beliefs and values towards politics (Almond and Verba, Pye); cognitive, affective and evaluative orientations; types - parochial, subject and participant, with the 'civic culture' as a mixed type suitable for stable democracy. Criticisms - Western-centric and static. Indian political culture combines high electoral participation with elements of deference to leaders, caste and community loyalties and a growing assertion by marginalised groups.

Political socialisation: the lifelong process of learning political values; agents - family, school, peer groups, mass media and social media, religious institutions, political parties, workplace, civil society and political events. It transmits political culture, creates support for the system and can also produce change. In Mizoram, the family, churches, schools and organisations like the YMA are important agents.

Political participation: activities to influence government - conventional (voting, campaigning, party work, contacting officials, petitions) and unconventional (protests, strikes, civil disobedience, social movements), as well as online participation; Milbrath's hierarchy and Verba and Nie's modes; factors - education, income, gender, caste, age, efficacy and political culture. In India, the poor and women vote in large numbers. Together, these concepts explain how citizens learn about, relate to and engage with political life.

sections.title: Social Stratification and Caste in Indian Politics

blocks.text:
Social stratification refers to persistent patterns of social inequality and ranking. In India, caste has historically been an important form of stratification alongside class, gender and other divisions.

Caste influences political mobilisation, candidate selection, representation and electoral behaviour. At the same time, democratic competition can alter caste relationships by providing new opportunities for political organisation and representation.

Caste and politics therefore influence one another rather than operating as completely separate spheres.

Social stratification: hierarchical arrangement of groups by unequal access to wealth, power and prestige; elements - differentiation, ranking, evaluation and rewarding; forms - slavery, estate, caste and class; theories - functionalist (Davis and Moore), Marxist (class conflict) and Weberian (class, status and party). In India, stratification is shaped by caste (purity and pollution, endogamy, hierarchy; Dumont, Srinivas), class, gender, religion, tribe and region. Constitutional measures and social movements have sought to reduce these inequalities.

Caste and politics: caste influences political mobilisation, party formation, candidate selection, voting behaviour and representation (Kothari's politicisation of caste; Rudolphs' caste associations; Srinivas's dominant caste). Democracy has transformed caste - lower castes have gained power through numbers (Jaffrelot's 'silent revolution'), the Mandal Commission and OBC politics, Dalit assertion (BSP), caste coalitions and reservations. Negative effects include vote-bank politics, caste conflicts and violence, and the use of caste identity over development issues.

Conclusion: caste and politics influence each other - caste shapes politics, and democratic politics changes caste by weakening ritual hierarchy and creating new forms of caste-based solidarity and competition. In tribal states such as Mizoram, caste does not operate, but clan, tribe, community and church shape political behaviour. Understanding stratification is essential for understanding the social bases of Indian democracy.
